title: Conjoint Analysis in Healthcare Management
text:
Conjoint analysis is a survey-based statistical technique used to understand how people make decisions when facing trade-offs between multiple attributes of a product or service. The core idea is simple: in real life, we rarely get everything we want. When choosing a health insurance plan, for example, we might prefer both low premiums AND low deductibles, but plans with low premiums often come with high deductibles. Conjoint analysis helps us understand how people navigate these trade-offs.
The term “conjoint” comes from “considered jointly”—we’re studying how attributes are evaluated together rather than in isolation. This is crucial because asking someone “Do you prefer low cost?” will always get a “yes,” but asking them to choose between a low-cost option with long wait times versus a high-cost option with short wait times reveals their true priorities.



Healthcare managers face constant decisions about service design:

Insurance plan design: What combination of premium, deductible, and coverage will attract enrollees?
Clinic operations: Should we prioritize shorter wait times or extended hours?
Telehealth services: Do patients value video consultations enough to pay more for them?
Hospital services: What amenities matter most to patients choosing where to receive care?

Conjoint analysis answers these questions by quantifying preferences. Instead of relying on intuition or simple surveys (“Would you like shorter wait times?”), conjoint analysis reveals how much each feature actually matters when people must make realistic trade-offs.



Conjoint analysis produces several valuable insights:


Part-worth utilities (also called “part-worths” or “utility scores”) are the building blocks of conjoint analysis. They represent the value or satisfaction that a person derives from a specific level of an attribute.
Think of it this way: every product or service is a bundle of attributes. A health insurance plan is a bundle of (premium, deductible, network size, etc.). The total utility (satisfaction) a person gets from a plan is the sum of the part-worth utilities for each attribute level in that plan.
Example: If the part-worth for “Large Network” is +3 and for “Small Network” is 0, then having a large network adds 3 utility units to the overall plan value. These numbers are relative—they only make sense in comparison to other levels of the same attribute.



Once we have part-worths, we can calculate how important each attribute is relative to others. This is done by looking at the range of utilities within each attribute (highest level minus lowest level) and comparing these ranges.
Example: If premium ranges from 0 to 5 utility units and network size ranges from 0 to 2 units, then premium has a larger impact on preferences and is therefore more “important.”



When price or cost is one of the attributes, we can convert utility differences into dollar values. This tells us how much extra a person would be willing to pay for an improvement in another attribute.
Example: If people would pay $50 more per month for a large network versus a small network, this helps managers decide whether investing in network expansion is worthwhile.



By knowing the utilities for each attribute level, we can predict what percentage of people would choose one option over another. This is invaluable for forecasting demand and competitive positioning.




This tutorial covers the two most common conjoint methods:



What respondents do: Rate each profile on a scale (e.g., 1-10)
Analysis approach: Linear regression (OLS)
Advantages: Simple to understand and implement
Limitations: Respondents may rate all options similarly, not revealing true trade-offs





What respondents do: Choose their preferred option from a set
Analysis approach: Logistic regression / Multinomial logit
Advantages: Mimics real-world decisions; forces explicit trade-offs
Limitations: Requires more sophisticated experimental design

Both methods ultimately produce the same types of outputs (part-worths, importance, WTP, market share), but choice-based conjoint is generally preferred in academic research and practice because it better reflects actual decision-making behavior (Louviere et al., 2000).

title: Conjoint Analysis in Healthcare Management
text:
Context and Background
One of the most studied applications of conjoint analysis in healthcare management is understanding how employees choose health insurance plans during open enrollment periods. This is a high-stakes decision for both employees (who will live with the plan for a year) and employers (who subsidize the plans).
Research has shown that employees often struggle with this decision due to the complexity of plan attributes. Studies by Sinaiko and Hirth (2011) in the Journal of Health Economics found that many employees make “dominated choices”—selecting plans that are objectively worse than alternatives on all dimensions. Understanding which attributes drive choices can help employers design better choice architectures and communication strategies.
Our example uses three key attributes that consistently appear in health plan conjoint studies:









Attribute
Level 1
Level 2
Why It Matters




Monthly Premium
$200
$300
Direct, visible cost paid every month


Annual Deductible
$500
$1,500
Amount paid before insurance kicks in


Network Size
Large
Small
Access to preferred doctors/hospitals

title: Conjoint Analysis in Healthcare Management
text:
Rating-Based Conjoint Analysis

Conceptual Overview
In rating-based conjoint analysis, we show respondents one hypothetical profile at a time and ask them to rate how attractive it is. For example:

Plan A: Monthly premium $200, Deductible $1,500, Small network
“On a scale from 1 to 10, how likely would you be to choose this plan?”

The respondent might give this a 4 out of 10. Then we show them another profile:

Plan B: Monthly premium $300, Deductible $500, Large network
Rating: 7 out of 10

By collecting ratings for multiple profiles across many respondents, we can use regression analysis to decompose these ratings into the contribution of each attribute. This works because we’ve systematically varied the attributes across profiles.


The Statistical Model
Rating-based conjoint uses ordinary least squares (OLS) regression, the same technique used in standard linear regression. The model assumes that a person’s rating is a linear combination of the utilities they assign to each attribute level:
\[\text{Rating} = \beta_0 + \beta_1(\text{Premium}) + \beta_2(\text{Deductible}) + \beta_3(\text{Network}) + \varepsilon\]
Where: - \(\beta_0\) is the intercept (baseline rating) - \(\beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3\) are the part-worth utilities for each attribute - \(\varepsilon\) is random error (individual variation, measurement error, etc.)
The coefficients we estimate ARE the part-worths. They tell us how much each unit change in an attribute affects the rating.


Generating the Experimental Design
First, we create all possible combinations of our attribute levels. With 3 attributes × 2 levels each, we have \(2^3 = 8\) possible profiles. This is called a full factorial design.

# Create full factorial design for insurance plans
# This generates all possible combinations of attribute levels
insurance_profiles <- expand.grid(
  premium = c(200, 300),
  deductible = c(500, 1500),
  network = c("Large", "Small")
)
insurance_profiles$profile_id <- 1:nrow(insurance_profiles)

# Display all 8 profiles
knitr::kable(insurance_profiles,
             col.names = c("Premium ($)", "Deductible ($)", "Network", "Profile ID"),
             caption = "Health Insurance Plan Profiles (Full Factorial Design)")

Simulating Respondent Data
In a real study, you would collect actual ratings from respondents. For this tutorial, we simulate data based on assumed “true” preferences. This allows us to verify that our analysis recovers the correct values.
Our assumed true preferences: - Premium: -0.02 utility per dollar (people prefer lower premiums) - Deductible: -0.003 utility per dollar (people prefer lower deductibles) - Network: +3 utility for Large network (people prefer larger networks)
These values reflect that a $100 difference in monthly premium (-0.02 × 100 = -2 utility) has about the same impact as a large vs. small network (+3 utility), suggesting people would pay roughly $150/month more for a large network.

# Simulate ratings from 100 respondents
# Each respondent rates all 8 profiles

n_respondents <- 100

rating_insurance <- data.frame()

for (resp in 1:n_respondents) {
  for (i in 1:nrow(insurance_profiles)) {
    # Calculate utility based on true preferences
    # The baseline of 50 centers our utility scale
    utility <- 50 +
      -0.02 * insurance_profiles$premium[i] +
      -0.003 * insurance_profiles$deductible[i] +
      3 * (insurance_profiles$network[i] == "Large") +
      rnorm(1, 0, 3)  # Add random noise to simulate individual variation

    # Convert utility to a 1-10 rating scale
    # We divide by 5 to scale appropriately and bound between 1 and 10
    rating <- round(pmin(pmax(utility / 5, 1), 10), 1)

    rating_insurance <- rbind(rating_insurance, data.frame(
      respondent_id = resp,
      profile_id = i,
      premium = insurance_profiles$premium[i],
      deductible = insurance_profiles$deductible[i],
      network = insurance_profiles$network[i],
      rating = rating
    ))
  }
}

# Show first few rows
cat("Dataset structure: ", nrow(rating_insurance), "rows (100 respondents × 8 profiles)\n\n")

Estimating Part-Worth Utilities
Now we use linear regression to estimate the part-worths. We code our variables numerically so the coefficients are directly interpretable:

Premium and deductible are kept as continuous variables (in dollars)
Network is coded as a binary indicator (1 = Large, 0 = Small)


# Create binary indicator for network size
rating_insurance <- rating_insurance %>%
  mutate(
    network_large = ifelse(network == "Large", 1, 0)
  )

# Fit linear regression model
model_rating_ins <- lm(rating ~ premium + deductible + network_large,
                       data = rating_insurance)

# Display full results
summary(model_rating_ins)

What do these coefficients mean?

Intercept (≈10): The baseline rating when all attributes are at their reference levels (but this is somewhat artificial given our coding)
Premium (≈-0.004): Each additional dollar in monthly premium decreases the rating by about 0.004 points. So a $100 increase reduces rating by 0.4 points.
Deductible (≈-0.0006): Each additional dollar in deductible decreases rating by about 0.0006 points. A $1,000 increase reduces rating by 0.6 points.
Network_large (≈0.6): Having a large network (vs. small) increases rating by about 0.6 points.

Note: Our recovered coefficients are scaled versions of the true utilities because we transformed utility to a 1-10 rating scale.


Calculating Attribute Importance
Attribute importance tells us which features have the biggest impact on preferences. The calculation is straightforward:

For each attribute, calculate the utility range: the difference between the highest and lowest part-worth values
Sum all the ranges
Express each range as a percentage of the total

Why use ranges? Because importance depends on how much the attribute levels differ. If we tested premiums of $200 vs. $201, premium would appear unimportant even though cost matters greatly to people. The range captures the actual impact given the levels we tested.

# Extract coefficients
coef_ins <- coef(model_rating_ins)

# Calculate utility ranges for each attribute
# For continuous variables: coefficient × (max level - min level)
# For binary variables: coefficient × 1

range_premium <- abs(coef_ins["premium"] * (300 - 200))  # $100 difference
range_deductible <- abs(coef_ins["deductible"] * (1500 - 500))  # $1000 difference
range_network <- abs(coef_ins["network_large"] * 1)  # Large vs Small

# Total range (sum of all ranges)
total_range <- range_premium + range_deductible + range_network

# Calculate importance as percentage
importance_rating_ins <- data.frame(
  attribute = c("Monthly Premium", "Annual Deductible", "Network Size"),
  utility_range = c(range_premium, range_deductible, range_network),
  importance_pct = c(range_premium, range_deductible, range_network) / total_range * 100
)

Calculating Willingness-to-Pay (WTP)
Willingness-to-pay converts the abstract utility values into concrete dollar amounts. This is possible because we included a price attribute (monthly premium) in our study.
The Logic: If we know how much utility a person gets from each attribute and how much utility they lose per dollar of cost, we can calculate the dollar amount that would exactly offset any utility gain.
The Formula: \[\text{WTP} = -\frac{\beta_{\text{attribute}}}{\beta_{\text{price}}}\]
The negative sign is needed because price coefficients are negative (people dislike higher prices) while beneficial attribute coefficients are positive.
Example Calculation: - Network coefficient = +0.6 (utility gain from large network) - Premium coefficient = -0.004 (utility loss per dollar) - WTP = -0.6 / (-0.004) = $150
This means respondents value a large network as much as they would value a $150 reduction in monthly premium.

# Extract relevant coefficients
beta_network <- coef_ins["network_large"]
beta_premium <- coef_ins["premium"]
beta_deductible <- coef_ins["deductible"]

# Calculate WTP for large network (vs small)
wtp_network <- -beta_network / beta_premium

# Calculate WTP for $1000 lower deductible
# (How much extra premium would someone pay to reduce deductible by $1000?)
wtp_deductible_reduction <- -(beta_deductible * -1000) / beta_premium

cat("Willingness-to-Pay Estimates:\n")

Practical Application: These WTP values help managers make cost-benefit decisions. If expanding the provider network costs the insurer $100 per member per month, and members are willing to pay $150 for it, the expansion could be profitable while also improving member satisfaction.


Market Share Simulation
One of the most powerful applications of conjoint analysis is predicting how the market would respond to different product configurations. Given the part-worth utilities, we can calculate the overall utility of any hypothetical product and predict choice shares.
The Process: 1. Define two (or more) competing options 2. Calculate total utility for each option by summing the part-worths 3. Convert utilities to choice probabilities using the logit formula
Why the Logit Formula?
The logit model comes from random utility theory (McFadden, 1974, who won the Nobel Prize for this work). It assumes that people choose the option with the highest utility, but there’s some randomness in choices. The formula is:
\[P(\text{Choose A}) = \frac{e^{U_A}}{e^{U_A} + e^{U_B}}\]
Where \(U_A\) and \(U_B\) are the total utilities of options A and B. This formula has nice properties: - If \(U_A > U_B\), then \(P(A) > 0.5\) (higher utility = higher probability) - If \(U_A = U_B\), then \(P(A) = 0.5\) (equal utilities = equal chances) - Probabilities always sum to 1

# Define two competing health plans
plan_A <- data.frame(
  name = "Premium Plan",
  premium = 250,
  deductible = 500,
  network_large = 1,
  description = "Mid-price, Low deductible, Large network"
)

plan_B <- data.frame(
  name = "Budget Plan",
  premium = 200,
  deductible = 1500,
  network_large = 0,
  description = "Low-price, High deductible, Small network"
)

# Calculate total utility for each plan using estimated coefficients
utility_A <- predict(model_rating_ins, plan_A)
utility_B <- predict(model_rating_ins, plan_B)

# Apply logit formula for market share
share_A <- exp(utility_A) / (exp(utility_A) + exp(utility_B))
share_B <- exp(utility_B) / (exp(utility_A) + exp(utility_B))

# Display results
market_share_rating <- data.frame(
  Plan = c(plan_A$name, plan_B$name),
  Description = c(plan_A$description, plan_B$description),
  Total_Utility = round(c(utility_A, utility_B), 3),
  Market_Share = paste0(round(c(share_A, share_B) * 100, 1), "%")
)

title: Conjoint Analysis in Healthcare Management
text:
Choice-Based Conjoint Analysis

Conceptual Overview
Choice-based conjoint (CBC), also known as a Discrete Choice Experiment (DCE), is considered the gold standard in conjoint analysis because it closely mimics real-world decision-making (Louviere, Hensher, & Swait, 2000).
Instead of rating profiles individually, respondents are shown choice sets containing two or more options and asked to pick their preferred one:

Choice Set 1:




Plan A
Plan B




Premium
$200
$300


Deductible
$1,500
$500


Network
Small
Large



Which plan would you choose? ☐ Plan A ☐ Plan B

By forcing a choice, we ensure that respondents make explicit trade-offs. Someone who wants both low premium AND low deductible must decide which matters more.


The Statistical Model
When choice sets have exactly two options (binary choice), we can use standard logistic regression. The key insight is that the choice depends on the difference in utilities between the options.
Mathematical Foundation: - Utility of Plan A: \(U_A = \beta_1 X_{A1} + \beta_2 X_{A2} + ...\) - Utility of Plan B: \(U_B = \beta_1 X_{B1} + \beta_2 X_{B2} + ...\) - Person chooses A if \(U_A > U_B\), i.e., if \(U_A - U_B > 0\)
This difference can be written as: \[U_A - U_B = \beta_1 (X_{A1} - X_{B1}) + \beta_2 (X_{A2} - X_{B2}) + ... = \beta_1 \Delta X_1 + \beta_2 \Delta X_2 + ...\]
So we model the probability of choosing A as a function of the attribute differences: \[P(\text{Choose A}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(β_1 \Delta X_1 + β_2 \Delta X_2 + ...)}}\]
This is exactly the logistic regression model! The coefficients we estimate are the part-worth utilities.


Generating Choice Data
We create choice sets by randomly pairing profiles, then simulate choices based on our assumed true utilities.

# Parameters for simulation
n_respondents <- 100
n_choice_sets <- 8  # Each respondent completes 8 choice tasks

choice_insurance <- data.frame()

for (resp in 1:n_respondents) {
  for (cs in 1:n_choice_sets) {
    # Randomly select two different profiles for this choice set
    profiles <- sample(1:8, 2)

    alt_A <- insurance_profiles[profiles[1], ]
    alt_B <- insurance_profiles[profiles[2], ]

    # Calculate utilities using same true values as before
    utility_A <- -0.02 * alt_A$premium -
                 0.003 * alt_A$deductible +
                 3 * (alt_A$network == "Large") +
                 rnorm(1, 0, 1)  # Random component

    utility_B <- -0.02 * alt_B$premium -
                 0.003 * alt_B$deductible +
                 3 * (alt_B$network == "Large") +
                 rnorm(1, 0, 1)

    # Choice: 1 if A chosen, 0 if B chosen
    choice_A <- as.integer(utility_A > utility_B)

    choice_insurance <- rbind(choice_insurance, data.frame(
      respondent_id = resp,
      choice_set = cs,
      # Alternative A attributes
      premium_A = alt_A$premium,
      deductible_A = alt_A$deductible,
      network_A = alt_A$network,
      # Alternative B attributes
      premium_B = alt_B$premium,
      deductible_B = alt_B$deductible,
      network_B = alt_B$network,
      # Choice outcome
      choice_A = choice_A
    ))
  }
}

Method 1: Binary Logistic Regression
For binary choices, we create difference variables and use standard logistic regression.

# Create difference variables (A minus B)
choice_insurance <- choice_insurance %>%
  mutate(
    diff_premium = premium_A - premium_B,
    diff_deductible = deductible_A - deductible_B,
    diff_network = (network_A == "Large") - (network_B == "Large")
  )

# Fit binary logistic regression
# Note: We remove the intercept (-1) because there's no inherent preference
# for "Alternative A" vs "Alternative B" - only the attributes matter
model_logit_ins <- glm(choice_A ~ diff_premium + diff_deductible + diff_network - 1,
                       data = choice_insurance,
                       family = binomial)

summary(model_logit_ins)

Interpreting Logistic Regression Coefficients:
The coefficients are on the log-odds scale. A coefficient of -0.08 for premium means that each additional dollar in premium for Plan A (compared to Plan B) decreases the log-odds of choosing A by 0.08.
More intuitively: - Negative premium coefficient: People prefer lower premiums (choose the cheaper option) - Negative deductible coefficient: People prefer lower deductibles - Positive network coefficient: People prefer larger networks


Method 2: Multinomial Logit (mlogit)
The mlogit package is designed for choice models and can handle: - More than 2 alternatives per choice set - Alternative-specific and individual-specific variables - More complex model specifications
For our binary choice data, mlogit should give similar results to standard logistic regression, confirming our approach.
Data Restructuring: mlogit requires data in “long” format where each row represents one alternative:

# Reshape data to long format
# Each choice set becomes two rows (one per alternative)
choice_long <- data.frame()

for (i in 1:nrow(choice_insurance)) {
  row <- choice_insurance[i, ]

  # Add Alternative A
  choice_long <- rbind(choice_long, data.frame(
    respondent_id = row$respondent_id,
    choice_set = paste0(row$respondent_id, "_", row$choice_set),
    alternative = "A",
    premium = row$premium_A,
    deductible = row$deductible_A,
    network_large = as.integer(row$network_A == "Large"),
    choice = row$choice_A
  ))

  # Add Alternative B
  choice_long <- rbind(choice_long, data.frame(
    respondent_id = row$respondent_id,
    choice_set = paste0(row$respondent_id, "_", row$choice_set),
    alternative = "B",
    premium = row$premium_B,
    deductible = row$deductible_B,
    network_large = as.integer(row$network_B == "Large"),
    choice = 1 - row$choice_A
  ))
}

# Convert to mlogit data format
# idx specifies: choice_set ID, and alternative ID
choice_mlogit <- dfidx(choice_long,
                       choice = "choice",
                       idx = c("choice_set", "alternative"))

# Fit conditional logit model
# The "| 0" means no alternative-specific constants
model_mlogit_ins <- mlogit(choice ~ premium + deductible + network_large | 0,
                           data = choice_mlogit)

summary(model_mlogit_ins)

Comparing the Two Approaches:
The coefficients from mlogit should be very close to those from binary logistic regression, which validates that both methods are equivalent for binary choice data. The mlogit approach is more flexible and is the standard for choice-based conjoint with 3+ alternatives.


Attribute Importance (Choice-Based)
The calculation is identical to rating-based conjoint: compute utility ranges and normalize.

# Use binary logistic regression coefficients

# Calculate utility ranges

range_deductible_c <- abs(coef_choice["diff_deductible"] * 1000)  # $1000 difference
range_network_c <- abs(coef_choice["diff_network"] * 1)  # Binary

total_range_c <- range_premium_c + range_deductible_c + range_network_c

importance_choice_ins <- data.frame(
  attribute = c("Monthly Premium", "Annual Deductible", "Network Size"),
  utility_range = c(range_premium_c, range_deductible_c, range_network_c),
  importance_pct = c(range_premium_c, range_deductible_c, range_network_c) / total_range_c * 100
)

coef_ml <- coef(model_mlogit_ins)

# Calculate utilities for the same two plans

               coef_ml["deductible"] * 500 +
               coef_ml["network_large"] * 1

utility_B_c <- coef_ml["premium"] * 200 +
               coef_ml["deductible"] * 1500 +
               coef_ml["network_large"] * 0

# Logit market share

share_B_c <- exp(utility_B_c) / (exp(utility_A_c) + exp(utility_B_c))

  Description = c("$250, $500 ded., Large network",

  Total_Utility = round(c(utility_A_c, utility_B_c), 3),

)

title: Conjoint Analysis in Healthcare Management
text:
Context and Background
The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the adoption of telehealth services, and healthcare organizations now face decisions about how to structure “hybrid” care models that combine virtual and in-person visits. Understanding patient preferences for telehealth attributes is crucial for designing services that people will actually use.
Research by Bürkin et al. (2023) in BMC Health Services Research used discrete choice experiments to examine patient preferences for primary care consultations, finding that attributes like wait time and consultation mode significantly influenced preferences. Our example is inspired by this and similar studies.

# Simulate ratings
# True utilities:
# Wait: +4 for same-day (patients strongly prefer immediate access)
# Mode: +2 for video (visual communication preferred over audio-only)
# Copay: -0.1 per dollar

n_respondents <- 100

rating_telehealth <- data.frame()

for (resp in 1:n_respondents) {
  for (i in 1:nrow(telehealth_profiles)) {
    utility <- 50 +
      4 * (telehealth_profiles$wait_time[i] == "Same-day") +
      2 * (telehealth_profiles$mode[i] == "Video") +
      -0.1 * telehealth_profiles$copay[i] +
      rnorm(1, 0, 2)

    rating <- round(pmin(pmax(utility / 5, 1), 10), 1)

    rating_telehealth <- rbind(rating_telehealth, data.frame(
      respondent_id = resp,
      profile_id = i,
      wait_time = telehealth_profiles$wait_time[i],
      mode = telehealth_profiles$mode[i],
      copay = telehealth_profiles$copay[i],
      rating = rating
    ))
  }
}

title: Conjoint Analysis in Healthcare Management
text:
Choice-Based Conjoint Analysis

Generate Choice Data

n_respondents <- 100
n_choice_sets <- 8

choice_telehealth <- data.frame()

for (resp in 1:n_respondents) {
  for (cs in 1:n_choice_sets) {
    profiles <- sample(1:8, 2)

    alt_A <- telehealth_profiles[profiles[1], ]
    alt_B <- telehealth_profiles[profiles[2], ]

    utility_A <- 4 * (alt_A$wait_time == "Same-day") +
                 2 * (alt_A$mode == "Video") -
                 0.1 * alt_A$copay + rnorm(1, 0, 0.5)
    utility_B <- 4 * (alt_B$wait_time == "Same-day") +
                 2 * (alt_B$mode == "Video") -
                 0.1 * alt_B$copay + rnorm(1, 0, 0.5)

    choice_A <- as.integer(utility_A > utility_B)

    choice_telehealth <- rbind(choice_telehealth, data.frame(
      respondent_id = resp,
      choice_set = cs,
      wait_A = alt_A$wait_time, mode_A = alt_A$mode, copay_A = alt_A$copay,
      wait_B = alt_B$wait_time, mode_B = alt_B$mode, copay_B = alt_B$copay,
      choice_A = choice_A
    ))
  }
}



Parameter Estimation

# Create difference variables
choice_telehealth <- choice_telehealth %>%
  mutate(
    diff_wait = (wait_A == "Same-day") - (wait_B == "Same-day"),
    diff_mode = (mode_A == "Video") - (mode_B == "Video"),
    diff_copay = copay_A - copay_B
  )

# Binary logistic regression
model_logit_th <- glm(choice_A ~ diff_wait + diff_mode + diff_copay - 1,
                      data = choice_telehealth, family = binomial)

summary(model_logit_th)


Call:
glm(formula = choice_A ~ diff_wait + diff_mode + diff_copay -

title: Conjoint Analysis in Healthcare Management
text:
Key Takeaways

Both methods yield similar part-worth utilities when properly designed, because they’re measuring the same underlying preferences
Choice-based is generally preferred in academic research and industry practice because it better mimics real decision-making and forces explicit trade-offs
Binary logistic regression works well for choice sets with exactly 2 alternatives—it’s simpler and equivalent to multinomial logit
The mlogit package extends to 3+ alternatives and offers more modeling flexibility
All outputs transfer across methods: Attribute importance, WTP, and market share calculations use the same formulas regardless of how part-worths were estimated
The key insight: Conjoint analysis transforms subjective preferences into quantitative data that managers can use for concrete decisions about pricing, feature prioritization, and competitive strategy

title: Conjoint Analysis in Healthcare Management
text:
Academic References

Green, P. E., & Srinivasan, V. (1990). Conjoint analysis in marketing: New developments with implications for research and practice. Journal of Marketing, 54(4), 3-19. (Classic overview of conjoint methods)
Louviere, J. J., Hensher, D. A., & Swait, J. D. (2000). Stated Choice Methods: Analysis and Applications. Cambridge University Press. (Comprehensive textbook on choice-based conjoint and discrete choice experiments)
McFadden, D. (1974). Conditional logit analysis of qualitative choice behavior. In P. Zarembka (Ed.), Frontiers in Econometrics (pp. 105-142). Academic Press. (Nobel Prize-winning work on discrete choice models)
Sinaiko, A. D., & Hirth, R. A. (2011). Consumers, health insurance and dominated choices. Journal of Health Economics, 30(2), 450-457. (Health insurance plan choice study)
Bürkin, F., et al. (2023). Patient preferences for primary care consultations: A discrete choice experiment. BMC Health Services Research, 23, 123. (Telehealth preferences study)

title: Conjoint Analysis in Healthcare Management
text:
Code and Examples
The examples and R code in this tutorial were developed specifically for this document. The scenarios (health insurance plans and telehealth programs) are inspired by the academic literature cited above but use simulated data generated with assumed “true” utility values to demonstrate the methods.
The data simulation approach (generating responses based on assumed utilities plus random error) is a standard technique for teaching conjoint analysis, as it allows students to verify that the estimated parameters recover the known true values.

title: Linear Regression in Healthcare Analytics
text:
In Part 1, we focused primarily on continuous predictors (e.g., age, severity scores). However, many important variables in healthcare are categorical:

Hospital type: Teaching vs. Community vs. Critical Access
Insurance type: Medicare, Medicaid, Private, Uninsured
Treatment protocol: Standard Care vs. Enhanced Recovery
Region: Northeast, South, Midwest, West

This section covers two essential extensions to linear regression:

Dummy Variables: How to include categorical predictors in regression
Interaction Effects: When the effect of one variable depends on another




Understanding these techniques allows you to:

Compare outcomes across hospital types or treatment groups
Determine if an intervention works differently for different patient populations
Make evidence-based decisions about resource allocation across categories
Design targeted interventions for specific subgroups

text:
2.1 The Challenge with Categorical Variables
Regression requires numerical inputs, but categorical variables are not inherently numerical. Simply assigning numbers (1, 2, 3) to categories implies an ordering and equal spacing that usually doesn’t exist.
Solution: Create dummy variables (also called indicator variables) that represent category membership using 0s and 1s.

2.2.1 Healthcare Example: Treatment Protocol Comparison
Let’s compare patient outcomes between a standard care protocol and an enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) protocol.

# Generate surgical patient data
n <- 200

surgical_data <- tibble(
  patient_id = 1:n,
  protocol = sample(c("Standard", "ERAS"), n, replace = TRUE),
  age = round(rnorm(n, 62, 12)),
  bmi = round(rnorm(n, 28, 5), 1),
  surgery_complexity = sample(1:3, n, replace = TRUE)  # 1=Low, 2=Medium, 3=High
) %>%
  mutate(
    age = pmax(30, pmin(age, 85)),
    bmi = pmax(18, pmin(bmi, 45)),
    # ERAS reduces LOS
    length_of_stay = round(
      3 +
      0.03 * age +
      0.05 * bmi +
      1.5 * surgery_complexity +
      -1.8 * (protocol == "ERAS") +  # ERAS effect
      rnorm(n, 0, 1),
      1
    ),
    length_of_stay = pmax(1, length_of_stay)
  )

# Summary by protocol
surgical_data %>%
  group_by(protocol) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_los = round(mean(length_of_stay), 2),
    sd_los = round(sd(length_of_stay), 2),
    min_los = min(length_of_stay),
    max_los = max(length_of_stay)
  ) %>%
  kable(caption = "Length of Stay by Treatment Protocol") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))

title: Linear Regression in Healthcare Analytics
text:
2.3 Multi-Level Categorical Variables
When a categorical variable has more than two levels, we need k-1 dummy variables (where k is the number of categories).

2.3.1 Why k-1 and Not k?
Including a dummy for every category would create perfect multicollinearity (the dummy variables would sum to 1 for every observation, which is perfectly correlated with the intercept).


2.3.2 Healthcare Example: Hospital Type Comparison
Let’s examine how hospital type affects 30-day readmission rates.

# Generate hospital data
n_hospitals <- 250

hospital_type_data <- tibble(
  hospital_id = 1:n_hospitals,
  hospital_type = sample(c("Teaching", "Community", "Critical Access"),
                        n_hospitals, replace = TRUE,
                        prob = c(0.25, 0.50, 0.25)),
  bed_count = case_when(
    hospital_type == "Teaching" ~ round(rnorm(n_hospitals, 400, 100)),
    hospital_type == "Community" ~ round(rnorm(n_hospitals, 200, 80)),
    hospital_type == "Critical Access" ~ round(rnorm(n_hospitals, 40, 15))
  ),
  avg_patient_severity = round(runif(n_hospitals, 1, 3), 2),
  nurse_per_patient = round(runif(n_hospitals, 2, 5), 2)
) %>%
  mutate(
    bed_count = pmax(10, bed_count),
    # Generate readmission rate
    readmission_rate = round(
      15 +
      2.5 * avg_patient_severity +
      -0.8 * nurse_per_patient +
      case_when(
        hospital_type == "Teaching" ~ -2.5,       # Reference in effect
        hospital_type == "Community" ~ 0,
        hospital_type == "Critical Access" ~ 3.0
      ) +
      rnorm(n_hospitals, 0, 2),
      1
    ),
    readmission_rate = pmax(5, pmin(readmission_rate, 30)),
    hospital_type = factor(hospital_type,
                          levels = c("Community", "Teaching", "Critical Access"))
  )

# Summary by hospital type
hospital_type_data %>%
  group_by(hospital_type) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_readmission = round(mean(readmission_rate), 2),
    sd_readmission = round(sd(readmission_rate), 2)
  ) %>%
  kable(caption = "Readmission Rates by Hospital Type") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))

title: Linear Regression in Healthcare Analytics
text:
3.1 What Are Interactions?
An interaction effect occurs when the effect of one variable on the outcome depends on the value of another variable.
Without interaction: \[Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \epsilon\]
With interaction: \[Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \beta_3 (X_1 \times X_2) + \epsilon\]
The interaction term \(\beta_3\) captures how the effect of \(X_1\) changes across levels of \(X_2\) (and vice versa).

title: Linear Regression in Healthcare Analytics
text:
3.2 Why Interactions Matter in Healthcare
Many healthcare relationships are conditional:

Treatment effectiveness varies by patient characteristics: A medication may work better for younger patients
Resource effects depend on hospital type: Additional staffing may have different impacts in teaching vs. community hospitals
Policy impacts vary by region: A new payment model may affect urban and rural hospitals differently

title: Linear Regression in Healthcare Analytics
text:
3.3 Continuous × Categorical Interaction

3.3.1 Healthcare Example: Does Staffing Effect Vary by Hospital Type?
Let’s test whether the effect of nurse staffing on patient satisfaction varies by hospital ownership type (for-profit vs. non-profit).

# Generate data for interaction example
n <- 300

satisfaction_data <- tibble(
  hospital_id = 1:n,
  ownership = sample(c("For-Profit", "Non-Profit"), n, replace = TRUE),
  nurse_ratio = round(runif(n, 2, 6), 2),
  patient_volume = round(rnorm(n, 500, 150)),
  avg_acuity = round(runif(n, 1, 3), 2)
) %>%
  mutate(
    patient_volume = pmax(100, patient_volume),
    # Interaction: staffing matters more in non-profit hospitals
    patient_satisfaction = round(
      50 +
      3 * nurse_ratio +                              # Base staffing effect
      5 * (ownership == "Non-Profit") +              # Non-profit baseline higher
      2.5 * nurse_ratio * (ownership == "Non-Profit") + # INTERACTION
      -0.01 * patient_volume +
      -3 * avg_acuity +
      rnorm(n, 0, 5),
      1
    ),
    patient_satisfaction = pmax(0, pmin(patient_satisfaction, 100)),
    ownership = factor(ownership, levels = c("For-Profit", "Non-Profit"))
  )



3.3.2 Visualizing the Potential Interaction
Before running the model, always visualize to see if an interaction might exist:

ggplot(satisfaction_data, aes(x = nurse_ratio, y = patient_satisfaction,
                              color = ownership)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("For-Profit" = "coral", "Non-Profit" = "steelblue")) +
  labs(
    x = "Nurse-to-Patient Ratio",
    y = "Patient Satisfaction Score",
    color = "Ownership Type",
    title = "Does Staffing Effect Differ by Hospital Ownership?",
    subtitle = "Different slopes suggest an interaction effect"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)







Figure 3: Potential interaction: different slopes suggest an interaction effect





Visual evidence: The slopes appear different. Staffing seems to have a stronger positive effect in Non-Profit hospitals.


3.3.3 Fitting the Interaction Model

# Model WITHOUT interaction (main effects only)
model_main <- lm(patient_satisfaction ~ nurse_ratio + ownership +
                 patient_volume + avg_acuity, data = satisfaction_data)

# Model WITH interaction
model_interact <- lm(patient_satisfaction ~ nurse_ratio * ownership +
                     patient_volume + avg_acuity, data = satisfaction_data)

# Alternative syntax for interaction: nurse_ratio + ownership + nurse_ratio:ownership

title: Linear Regression in Healthcare Analytics
text:
3.4 Categorical × Categorical Interaction
Interactions can also occur between two categorical variables.

3.4.1 Healthcare Example: Treatment Effect Varies by Insurance Type
Does the effectiveness of a diabetes management program differ by patient insurance type?

# Generate data
n <- 400

diabetes_data <- tibble(
  patient_id = 1:n,
  treatment = sample(c("Standard Care", "Intensive Program"), n, replace = TRUE),
  insurance = sample(c("Medicare", "Medicaid", "Private"), n, replace = TRUE,
                    prob = c(0.4, 0.3, 0.3)),
  baseline_a1c = round(rnorm(n, 8.5, 1.2), 1),
  age = round(rnorm(n, 60, 12))
) %>%
  mutate(
    baseline_a1c = pmax(6, pmin(baseline_a1c, 12)),
    age = pmax(30, pmin(age, 85)),
    # Generate A1c reduction with interaction
    a1c_reduction = round(
      0.5 +
      0.3 * (treatment == "Intensive Program") +   # Base treatment effect
      0.2 * (insurance == "Private") +              # Private insurance effect
      0.1 * (insurance == "Medicare") +
      # Interactions: treatment works better with Private insurance
      0.8 * (treatment == "Intensive Program") * (insurance == "Private") +
      0.3 * (treatment == "Intensive Program") * (insurance == "Medicare") +
      0.05 * baseline_a1c +
      rnorm(n, 0, 0.4),
      2
    ),
    a1c_reduction = pmax(0, a1c_reduction),
    treatment = factor(treatment, levels = c("Standard Care", "Intensive Program")),
    insurance = factor(insurance, levels = c("Medicaid", "Medicare", "Private"))
  )



3.4.2 Fitting and Interpreting

# Fit model with interaction
model_diabetes <- lm(a1c_reduction ~ treatment * insurance + baseline_a1c + age,
                     data = diabetes_data)

title: Linear Regression in Healthcare Analytics
text:
3.5 Continuous × Continuous Interaction
Interactions can also occur between two continuous variables.

3.5.1 Healthcare Example: Age Moderates Treatment Duration Effect
Does the benefit of longer physical therapy duration depend on patient age?

# Generate data
n <- 250

pt_data <- tibble(
  patient_id = 1:n,
  pt_sessions = round(runif(n, 4, 24)),
  age = round(runif(n, 25, 80)),
  baseline_function = round(runif(n, 30, 70))
) %>%
  mutate(
    # Interaction: PT sessions more effective for younger patients
    function_improvement = round(
      5 +
      1.2 * pt_sessions +
      -0.1 * age +
      -0.03 * pt_sessions * age +  # Negative interaction
      0.3 * baseline_function +
      rnorm(n, 0, 5),
      1
    ),
    function_improvement = pmax(0, function_improvement)
  )

# Fit model
model_pt <- lm(function_improvement ~ pt_sessions * age + baseline_function,
               data = pt_data)

summary(model_pt)

For continuous × continuous interactions, we typically show the effect at different levels of the moderator:

# Create prediction data for different age groups
age_levels <- c(30, 50, 70)

pred_pt <- expand_grid(
  pt_sessions = seq(4, 24, by = 1),
  age = age_levels,
  baseline_function = mean(pt_data$baseline_function)
) %>%
  mutate(
    predicted = predict(model_pt, newdata = .),
    age_group = paste("Age", age)

ggplot(pred_pt, aes(x = pt_sessions, y = predicted, color = factor(age))) +
  geom_line(size = 1.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("30" = "steelblue", "50" = "orange", "70" = "darkred"),
                    labels = c("Age 30", "Age 50", "Age 70")) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of PT Sessions",
    y = "Predicted Function Improvement",
    color = "Patient Age",
    title = "Interaction: PT Sessions × Age",
    subtitle = "More sessions help younger patients more"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)







Figure 7: PT sessions effect varies by patient age





Interpretation: The positive effect of additional PT sessions on functional improvement is stronger for younger patients. For a 30-year-old, each additional session provides substantially more benefit than for a 70-year-old.

title: Linear Regression in Healthcare Analytics
text:
4.1 When to Include Interactions
Include interactions when:

Theory or prior research suggests the effect should vary
Visual inspection shows different slopes for different groups
You have sufficient sample size (interactions require larger samples)

Avoid over-fitting: Don’t include interactions just to “improve R².” Only include interactions with theoretical justification.

4.2 Centering Variables
For models with interactions, centering continuous variables (subtracting the mean) improves interpretability:

    patient_volume_c = patient_volume - mean(patient_volume)

# Model with centered variables
model_centered <- lm(patient_satisfaction ~ nurse_ratio_c * ownership +
                     patient_volume_c + avg_acuity, data = satisfaction_data)

  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(., 3))) %>%

text:
4.3 Sample Size Requirements
Interactions require larger sample sizes because:

They partition the data into subgroups
They add parameters to estimate
They can have smaller effect sizes

Rule of thumb: Have at least 15-20 observations per combination of categorical variables involved in the interaction.

set.seed(456)
n <- 350

quality_data <- tibble(
  hospital_id = 1:n,

title: Linear Regression in Healthcare Analytics
text:
6.1 Key Takeaways

6.1.1 Dummy Variables

Represent categorical variables using 0/1 indicator variables
For k categories, create k-1 dummy variables
Coefficients represent differences from the reference category
Change reference category with relevel() to make different comparisons



6.1.2 Interaction Effects

Occur when the effect of one variable depends on another variable
Include interaction term: X1 * X2 or X1:X2
Test significance by comparing models with and without interaction
Main effects change meaning when interaction is present



6.1.3 Interpretation Guidelines
For interactions between continuous (X) and categorical (Z) variables:

Main effect of X: Effect of X when Z = reference category
Main effect of Z: Effect of Z when X = 0 (or mean if centered)
Interaction: How much the effect of X changes for other levels of Z

For interactions between two categorical variables:

Use marginal means to compare all combinations
Visualize with grouped bar charts or interaction plots



6.1.4 Healthcare Applications

Compare outcomes across hospital types, regions, or treatment groups
Test whether interventions work differently for different populations
Identify which patient subgroups benefit most from specific treatments
Understand how organizational characteristics moderate the effects of investments

title: Linear Regression in Healthcare Analytics
text:
6.2 Best Practices

Visualize before modeling - Look for different slopes or patterns
Have theoretical justification - Don’t fish for interactions
Center continuous variables - Improves interpretability
Check sample sizes - Need adequate observations per subgroup
Report results clearly - Calculate simple slopes, create visualizations

title: Mean Comparison 2: One-Way and Repeated-Measure ANOVA
text:
We frequently need to compare outcomes across more than two groups. Let’s think about these scenarios:

Comparing patient satisfaction scores across five different hospital departments
Evaluating readmission rates among three different care coordination models
Assessing staff performance across four different training programs
Tracking patient outcomes at multiple time points during recovery

While t-tests are excellent for comparing two groups, they cannot handle these multi-group comparisons. This is where Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) becomes essential. ANOVA allows us to determine whether there are statistically significant differences among three or more group means in a single test.



You might wonder: “Why not just run multiple t-tests to compare each pair of groups?” This approach is tempting but fundamentally flawed due to the familywise error rate problem.


Each time we conduct a statistical test at α = 0.05, we accept a 5% chance of making a Type I error (false positive; concluding there’s a difference when there isn’t one). When we perform multiple tests, these error rates increase.
The probability of Type I error across multiple tests is:
\[P(\text{at least one Type I error}) = 1 - (1 - \alpha)^k\]
Where \(k\) is the number of comparisons.









For example, with just 4 groups, you would need 6 pairwise t-tests. The familywise error rate becomes: \[1 - (0.95)^6 = 0.265 = 26.5\%\]
This means you have a 26.5% chance of finding at least one “significant” difference by pure chance—far from the 5% we intended!



ANOVA tests all groups simultaneously with a single test, maintaining the Type I error rate at our desired α level (in our class, 5%). If ANOVA finds a significant difference, we then use post-hoc tests with appropriate corrections to identify which specific groups differ.




This document covers two fundamental ANOVA designs:








ANOVA Type
Purpose
Example




One-Way ANOVA
Compare means across 3+ independent groups
Comparing satisfaction scores across 4 hospital departments


Repeated-Measures ANOVA
Compare means across 3+ related measurements on the same subjects
Tracking pain scores at baseline, 1 month, 3 months, and 6 months

text:
You might wonder: “Why not just run multiple t-tests to compare each pair of groups?” This approach is tempting but fundamentally flawed due to the familywise error rate problem.


Each time we conduct a statistical test at α = 0.05, we accept a 5% chance of making a Type I error (false positive; concluding there’s a difference when there isn’t one). When we perform multiple tests, these error rates increase.
The probability of Type I error across multiple tests is:
\[P(\text{at least one Type I error}) = 1 - (1 - \alpha)^k\]
Where \(k\) is the number of comparisons.









For example, with just 4 groups, you would need 6 pairwise t-tests. The familywise error rate becomes: \[1 - (0.95)^6 = 0.265 = 26.5\%\]
This means you have a 26.5% chance of finding at least one “significant” difference by pure chance—far from the 5% we intended!



ANOVA tests all groups simultaneously with a single test, maintaining the Type I error rate at our desired α level (in our class, 5%). If ANOVA finds a significant difference, we then use post-hoc tests with appropriate corrections to identify which specific groups differ.

title: Mean Comparison 2: One-Way and Repeated-Measure ANOVA
text:
What is it?
A one-way ANOVA (Analysis of Variance) tests whether there are statistically significant differences among the means of three or more independent groups. The “one-way” refers to having one independent variable (factor) with multiple levels (groups).
ANOVA actually analyzes variance to make inferences about means. It works by partitioning the total variability in the data into:

Between-group variance: Differences among group means
Within-group variance: Differences among individuals within groups

If the between-group variance is substantially larger than the within-group variance, we conclude that the group means are significantly different.

Key Components

One independent variable (factor) with 3+ levels
Independent groups: Each observation belongs to only one group
Continuous dependent variable: The outcome measure

title: Mean Comparison 2: One-Way and Repeated-Measure ANOVA
text:
When to Use It
One-way ANOVA is appropriate whenever you need to compare means across three or more distinct, unrelated groups:

Comparing patient outcomes across different treatment protocols
Evaluating staff performance across multiple departments
Comparing operational metrics across several facilities
Assessing patient satisfaction across various service lines
Comparing cost efficiency across different care models

section: Scenario 1: Patient Satisfaction Across Hospital Departments
text:
Scenario 1: Patient Satisfaction Across Hospital Departments
A hospital administrator wants to evaluate patient satisfaction across four departments: Emergency, Cardiology, Orthopedics, and Oncology. Each department has implemented different patient experience initiatives, and leadership wants to know if satisfaction levels differ significantly.

title: Mean Comparison 2: One-Way and Repeated-Measure ANOVA
text:
The Formula
The one-way ANOVA calculates an F-statistic:
\[F = \frac{\text{Between-group variance}}{\text{Within-group variance}} = \frac{MS_{between}}{MS_{within}}\]
Where:

Mean Square Between (\(MS_{between}\)): Average variance among group means \[MS_{between} = \frac{SS_{between}}{df_{between}} = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{k} n_j(\bar{X}_j - \bar{X}_{grand})^2}{k-1}\]
Mean Square Within (\(MS_{within}\)): Average variance within groups \[MS_{within} = \frac{SS_{within}}{df_{within}} = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}(X_{ij} - \bar{X}_j)^2}{N-k}\]

Where:

\(k\) = number of groups
\(n_j\) = sample size of group \(j\)
\(N\) = total sample size
\(\bar{X}_j\) = mean of group \(j\)
\(\bar{X}_{grand}\) = overall mean (grand mean)


Understanding the F-Statistic
The F-statistic is a ratio:

F ≈ 1: Between-group variance is similar to within-group variance → group means are likely not different
F >> 1: Between-group variance is much larger than within-group variance → group means are likely different

Think of it this way: If the groups truly have different means, the variance between their means should be larger than what we would expect from random sampling variation (within-group variance).

title: Mean Comparison 2: One-Way and Repeated-Measure ANOVA
text:
Manual Calculation: Understanding the F-Statistic
Let’s manually calculate the ANOVA components to understand what the test is actually doing. This mirrors the manual calculation approach we used for t-tests.

# Step 1: Calculate group means and overall mean
mean_emergency <- mean(emergency)
mean_cardiology <- mean(cardiology)
mean_orthopedics <- mean(orthopedics)
mean_oncology <- mean(oncology)
grand_mean <- mean(satisfaction_data$score)

# Step 2: Calculate Sum of Squares Between Groups (SSB)
n_per_group <- 20
ssb <- n_per_group * (
  (mean_emergency - grand_mean)^2 +
  (mean_cardiology - grand_mean)^2 +
  (mean_orthopedics - grand_mean)^2 +
  (mean_oncology - grand_mean)^2
)

# Step 3: Calculate Sum of Squares Within Groups (SSW)
ssw <- sum((emergency - mean_emergency)^2) +
       sum((cardiology - mean_cardiology)^2) +
       sum((orthopedics - mean_orthopedics)^2) +
       sum((oncology - mean_oncology)^2)

# Step 4: Calculate degrees of freedom
k <- 4  # number of groups
n_total <- nrow(satisfaction_data)
df_between <- k - 1
df_within <- n_total - k

# Step 5: Calculate Mean Squares
ms_between <- ssb / df_between
ms_within <- ssw / df_within

# Step 6: Calculate F-statistic
f_statistic <- ms_between / ms_within

# Step 7: Calculate p-value
p_value <- 1 - pf(f_statistic, df_between, df_within)



Manual ANOVA Calculation:


========================


Group Means:


  Emergency:     7.51 


  Cardiology:    7.99 


  Orthopedics:   7.76 


  Oncology:      8.13 


  Grand Mean:    7.85 


Sum of Squares:


  Between groups (SSB):  4.45 


  Within groups (SSW):   21.93 


Degrees of Freedom:


  Between:  3 


  Within:   76 


Mean Squares:


  MS Between:  1.48 


  MS Within:   0.29 


F-statistic:  5.14 


p-value:      0.00272 



Understanding What These Numbers Mean

Between-group variance (MS Between = 1.48): This measures how much the department means differ from each other. Larger values indicate greater differences among departments.
Within-group variance (MS Within = 0.29): This measures the typical variation among patients within the same department. It represents “noise” or natural variation.
F-statistic (F = 5.14): The ratio of between-group to within-group variance. Our F-value of 5.14 means the between-group variance is 5.14 times larger than the within-group variance, suggesting real differences exist among departments.

text:
Conducting One-Way ANOVA in R

# Perform one-way ANOVA
anova_result <- aov(score ~ department, data = satisfaction_data)
summary(anova_result)

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value  Pr(>F)   
department   3  4.451  1.4838   5.143 0.00272 **
Residuals   76 21.928  0.2885                   
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1



Interpreting the ANOVA Table

Df (Degrees of Freedom):

Between groups: \(k - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3\)
Within groups: \(N - k = 80 - 4 = 76\)

Sum Sq (Sum of Squares): Total variance explained by the factor (between) vs. unexplained variance (within)
Mean Sq (Mean Square): Sum of Squares divided by degrees of freedom
F value: The test statistic—ratio of between-group to within-group variance
Pr(>F): The p-value—probability of observing this F-value if all group means were truly equal



Conclusion from ANOVA
With F = 5.14 and p < 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis. There are statistically significant differences in patient satisfaction among the four departments.
But which departments differ from each other? The ANOVA tells us that differences exist but not where they are. For this, we need post-hoc tests.

title: Mean Comparison 2: One-Way and Repeated-Measure ANOVA
text:
Post-Hoc Tests: Tukey’s HSD
When ANOVA is significant, we use post-hoc tests to identify which specific groups differ. Tukey’s Honest Significant Difference (HSD) test compares all possible pairs while controlling the familywise error rate.

What is Tukey’s HSD?
Tukey’s HSD is designed to solve a specific problem: How do we compare all pairs of groups while maintaining our overall Type I error rate at α = 0.05?
Key features:

Tests all pairwise comparisons - For k groups, it tests all \(\frac{k(k-1)}{2}\) possible pairs

4 groups → 6 comparisons
5 groups → 10 comparisons

Controls familywise error rate - Your overall chance of making at least one Type I error stays at 5% across ALL comparisons (not 5% per comparison)
Uses the studentized range distribution - More appropriate than t-distribution for multiple comparisons

The HSD critical value:
\[HSD = q_{\alpha, k, df_{error}} \times \sqrt{\frac{MS_{within}}{n}}\]
Where:

\(q_{\alpha, k, df_{error}}\) = critical value from studentized range distribution
\(MS_{within}\) = mean square error from ANOVA
\(n\) = sample size per group
\(k\) = number of groups

If the absolute difference between two group means exceeds HSD, that difference is statistically significant.


Conducting Tukey’s HSD in R Using emmeans
Now let’s use the emmeans package, which is the modern standard for post-hoc testing:

# Step 1: Calculate estimated marginal means
emm_dept <- emmeans(anova_result, ~ department)
emm_dept

 department  emmean   SE df lower.CL upper.CL
 Cardiology    7.99 0.12 76     7.75     8.23
 Emergency     7.51 0.12 76     7.27     7.75
 Oncology      8.13 0.12 76     7.89     8.37
 Orthopedics   7.75 0.12 76     7.52     7.99

Confidence level used: 0.95 

# Step 2: Perform pairwise comparisons with Tukey adjustment
tukey_pairs <- pairs(emm_dept, adjust = "tukey")
tukey_pairs

 contrast                 estimate   SE df t.ratio p.value
 Cardiology - Emergency      0.480 0.17 76   2.826  0.0300
 Cardiology - Oncology      -0.140 0.17 76  -0.824  0.8428
 Cardiology - Orthopedics    0.235 0.17 76   1.384  0.5135

 Oncology - Orthopedics      0.375 0.17 76   2.208  0.1304

P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 4 estimates 




Interpreting Tukey’s HSD Output
Each row in the output shows a pairwise comparison:

contrast: Which two groups are being compared
estimate: Difference between group means
SE: Standard error of the difference
df: Degrees of freedom
t.ratio: Test statistic
p.value: Adjusted p-value (controlling for multiple comparisons)

Decision rule:

If p.value < 0.05, those groups are significantly different

text:
Example 2: Comparing Care Coordination Models
A health system wants to evaluate three different care coordination models for managing patients with chronic conditions. They measure 30-day readmission rates (%) across facilities using each model.
Real-world context: Studies have shown that different care coordination approaches produce varying outcomes, with community health worker interventions and transition care coordinator models demonstrating significant reductions in hospital readmissions. The comparative effectiveness of different models remains an important question for resource allocation.
Model A: Nurse-Led Telephone Follow-Up

Registered nurses call patients within 48 hours of discharge
Phone-based medication reconciliation and education
Identification of red flags or concerning symptoms
Lowest resource intensity but limited ability to assess home environment
Relies on patient self-report

Model B: Community Health Worker (CHW) Home Visits

Trained community health workers conduct in-person home visits within 72 hours
Visual assessment of home environment, medication compliance, and social determinants
Can connect patients to community resources (food, transportation, social services)
Cultural concordance often improves trust and communication
Higher resource intensity than phone calls

Model C: Integrated Care Team with Digital Monitoring

Multidisciplinary team (nurse, pharmacist, social worker) coordinates care
Patients receive remote monitoring devices (blood pressure, weight, pulse oximetry)
Daily automated data transmission to care team
Algorithm-driven alerts trigger proactive interventions
Weekly team huddles to review high-risk patients
Highest resource intensity but most comprehensive approach

Do these three care coordination models differ significantly in their effectiveness at reducing 30-day hospital readmissions?

# 30-day readmission rates (%) by care coordination model
model_A <- c(12.5, 14.2, 11.8, 13.6, 12.9, 14.8, 11.5, 13.2, 12.7, 14.1,
             13.4, 12.2, 14.5, 11.9, 13.8, 12.4, 14.3, 13.1, 12.6, 13.9)

model_B <- c(10.2, 11.5, 9.8, 10.9, 11.2, 10.5, 9.6, 11.8, 10.3, 11.1,
             10.7, 9.9, 11.4, 10.1, 10.8, 11.6, 9.7, 10.6, 11.3, 10.4)

model_C <- c(8.5, 9.2, 7.8, 8.9, 9.5, 8.2, 7.6, 9.1, 8.6, 8.8,
             9.3, 8.1, 8.7, 7.9, 9.4, 8.3, 7.7, 9.0, 8.4, 8.9)

# Create data frame
readmission_data <- data.frame(
  rate = c(model_A, model_B, model_C),
  model = factor(rep(c("Model A: Nurse Phone", "Model B: CHW Visits",
                       "Model C: Integrated"), each = 20))
)











# Perform ANOVA
anova_readmit <- aov(rate ~ model, data = readmission_data)
summary(anova_readmit)

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)    
model        2 209.91  104.95   183.3 <2e-16 ***
Residuals   57  32.63    0.57                   
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1



Interpreting the ANOVA Results
With F = 183.32 and p < 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis. There are statistically significant differences in 30-day readmission rates among the three care coordination models.
Observed mean readmission rates:

Model A (Nurse Phone): 13.17%
Model B (CHW Visits): 10.67%

But which specific models differ from each other? Let’s examine the post-hoc tests.

title: Mean Comparison 2: One-Way and Repeated-Measure ANOVA
text:
What is it?
A repeated-measures ANOVA (also called within-subjects ANOVA) tests whether there are significant differences across three or more related measurements on the same respondents. This design is the extension of the paired t-test to situations involving more than two time points, measurements, or conditions.
The key advantage of repeated-measures designs is that each respondent serves as their own control, which reduces error variance and increases statistical power. By tracking the same individuals over time, we eliminate individual differences as a source of variability.

Key Components

Same subjects, respondents, patients measured multiple times
Three or more measurement occasions or conditions
Related observations: Each subject contributes data to all conditions

title: Mean Comparison 2: One-Way and Repeated-Measure ANOVA
text:
When to Use It
Repeated-measures ANOVA is appropriate for:

Longitudinal studies: Tracking patients at multiple time points

Pain scores at baseline (month 0), 1 month, 3 months, 6 months
HbA1c levels across quarterly clinic visits

Within-subject experiments: Testing same subjects under different conditions

Response to different medication dosages
Performance under different shift schedules

Quality improvement tracking: Monitoring metrics over multiple periods

Hospital safety scores across quarters
Patient satisfaction before, during, and after initiative implementation

title: Mean Comparison 2: One-Way and Repeated-Measure ANOVA
text:
Scenario 1: Diabetes Management Program

Background and Context
A healthcare organization implements a comprehensive diabetes management program for patients with poorly controlled Type 2 diabetes. The program includes:

Monthly nurse educator visits for medication management and lifestyle coaching
Quarterly endocrinologist consultations for treatment plan adjustments
Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) with remote monitoring by care team
Nutritionist consultations for personalized meal planning
Group support sessions for peer learning and motivation



The Outcome Measure: HbA1c
What is HbA1c?

Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) measures average blood glucose over the past 2-3 months
Reported as a percentage (e.g., 7.5%)
Clinical targets:

Normal: < 5.7%
Prediabetes: 5.7-6.4%
Diabetes: ≥ 6.5%
Treatment goal for most diabetics: < 7.0%

Why it matters: Each 1% reduction in HbA1c is associated with significant reductions in diabetes complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy)



Study Design
The organization tracks HbA1c levels for 25 enrolled patients at four time points:

Baseline: Before program enrollment (typical range: 8-10% for poorly controlled diabetes)
3 months: Initial follow-up (early response to intervention)
6 months: Mid-program (sustained adherence check)
12 months: Program completion (long-term effectiveness)



Why Use Repeated-Measures ANOVA?
This is a perfect scenario for repeated-measures ANOVA because:

Same patients tracked over time - Each patient serves as their own control
Multiple time points - Four measurements (more than two)
Reduces individual variability - Some patients naturally have higher HbA1c than others; repeated measures accounts for this
Efficient use of resources - We need only 25 patients instead of 100 (25 per group × 4 groups) if we used one-way ANOVA
Longitudinal question - We want to know if HbA1c changes over time within the same individuals



Research Questions
Primary: Does HbA1c change significantly over the course of the 12-month program?
Secondary (if significant): - At which time points do we see significant improvements? - Do patients reach the clinical target of < 7.0% by 12 months? - Is the improvement sustained or does it plateau?
Management Implications: - If effective: Continue funding and expand program - If not effective: Investigate barriers (adherence, program design, patient selection) - Identify when improvements occur to optimize resource allocation

title: Mean Comparison 2: One-Way and Repeated-Measure ANOVA
text:
The Formula
Repeated-measures ANOVA partitions variance differently than one-way ANOVA to account for the correlation between measurements on the same subject:
\[F = \frac{MS_{time}}{MS_{error}}\]
Where:

\(MS_{time}\) = Mean square for the time (or condition) effect
\(MS_{error}\) = Mean square for error (residual variation after removing both subject and time effects)


Formulas for Sum of Squares Components
To calculate the variance components in repeated-measures ANOVA, we need these formulas:
0. Total Sum of Squares (SS_total):
\[SS_{total} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{t} (X_{ij} - \bar{X}_{grand})^2\]
Where:

\(X_{ij}\) = observation for subject \(i\) at time point \(j\)
\(\bar{X}_{grand}\) = overall grand mean (across all subjects and all time points)
\(n\) = number of subjects
\(t\) = number of time points

What it measures: Total variation in all observations from the grand mean. This is the “starting point” that we partition into components.
1. Sum of Squares for Time Effect (SS_time):
\[SS_{time} = n \sum_{j=1}^{t} (\bar{X}_j - \bar{X}_{grand})^2\]
Where:

\(n\) = number of subjects
\(t\) = number of time points
\(\bar{X}_j\) = mean at time point \(j\) (averaging across all subjects)
\(\bar{X}_{grand}\) = overall grand mean (across all subjects and all time points)

What it measures: How much do the time point means differ from the overall mean?
2. Sum of Squares Between-Subjects (SS_subjects):
\[SS_{subjects} = t \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\bar{X}_i - \bar{X}_{grand})^2\]
Where:

\(\bar{X}_i\) = mean for subject \(i\) (averaging across all time points)

What it measures: How much do individual subjects differ from the overall mean? (This gets removed from the error term!)
3. Sum of Squares Error (SS_error):
\[SS_{error} = SS_{total} - SS_{subjects} - SS_{time}\]
Or, calculated directly:
\[SS_{error} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{t} (X_{ij} - \bar{X}_i - \bar{X}_j + \bar{X}_{grand})^2\]
Where:

\(X_{ij}\) = observation for subject \(i\) at time \(j\)
\(\bar{X}_i\) = mean for subject \(i\)
\(\bar{X}_j\) = mean for time \(j\)
\(\bar{X}_{grand}\) = grand mean

What it measures: Random variation left over after removing both subject differences and time effects.
Notice that \(SS_{error}\) is calculated by subtracting out both subject means AND time means. This is why it’s smaller than one-way ANOVA error—we’ve removed the between-subjects variance!


Calculating the F-Statistic
The F-statistic tests whether the time effect is larger than random error:
\[F = \frac{MS_{time}}{MS_{error}} = \frac{SS_{time}/df_{time}}{SS_{error}/df_{error}}\]
Where:

\(df_{time} = t - 1\) (number of time points minus 1)
\(df_{error} = (n-1)(t-1)\) (subjects - 1) × (time points - 1)

Interpretation:

F ≈ 1: Time effect similar to random variation → no significant change
F >> 1: Time effect much larger than random variation → significant change over time

title: Mean Comparison 2: One-Way and Repeated-Measure ANOVA
text:
Example: Diabetes Management Program

# HbA1c levels (%) for 25 patients at 4 time points

# Generate realistic data showing improvement over time

title: Mean Comparison 2: One-Way and Repeated-Measure ANOVA
text:
Conducting Repeated-Measures ANOVA in R
For repeated-measures ANOVA, we need to specify the error term to account for the within-subjects design:

# Repeated-measures ANOVA
# Error(patient_id/time) specifies that time is within subjects
rm_anova <- aov(hba1c ~ time + Error(patient_id/time), data = diabetes_data)
summary(rm_anova)


Error: patient_id
          Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
Residuals 24  83.75    3.49               

Error: patient_id:time
          Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)    
time       3 14.780   4.927   84.92 <2e-16 ***
Residuals 72  4.177   0.058                   
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1



Interpreting the Output
Understanding the R Output:

time row: Tests whether mean HbA1c differs across time points
Df = 3: Degrees of freedom for time (4 time points - 1)
F value: Ratio of time effect variance to residual variance
Pr(>F): p-value for the time effect



Conclusion and Clinical Interpretation
Statistical Conclusion:
With a significant F-test (p < 0.05), we reject the null hypothesis. HbA1c levels changed significantly over the course of the 12-month diabetes management program.
Clinical Interpretation:
Mean HbA1c levels by time point:

Baseline: 8.38% (poorly controlled diabetes)
3 Months: 7.96%
6 Months: 7.64%
12 Months: 7.34%

Overall improvement: 1.04 percentage points (a 12.4% relative reduction from baseline)
Clinical significance:

Patients started with poorly controlled diabetes (average 8.38%)
By 12 months, average HbA1c approached or achieved the treatment goal of <7.0%
This magnitude of reduction is associated with meaningful decreases in long-term complications

But which specific time points differ? We need post-hoc tests to determine when significant improvements occurred.

title: Mean Comparison 2: One-Way and Repeated-Measure ANOVA
text:
Post-Hoc Tests for Repeated Measures
To identify which time points differ, we use pairwise comparisons with p-value adjustment:

# Extract estimated marginal means
emm_time <- emmeans(rm_anova, ~ time)
emm_time

 time      emmean    SE   df lower.CL upper.CL
 Baseline    8.38 0.191 26.4     7.98     8.77
 3 Months    7.96 0.191 26.4     7.57     8.35
 6 Months    7.64 0.191 26.4     7.25     8.03
 12 Months   7.34 0.191 26.4     6.95     7.73

Warning: EMMs are biased unless design is perfectly balanced 
Confidence level used: 0.95 

# Pairwise comparisons with Tukey adjustment
pairs(emm_time, adjust = "tukey")

 contrast             estimate     SE df t.ratio p.value
 Baseline - 3 Months     0.416 0.0681 72   6.106  <.0001
 Baseline - 6 Months     0.736 0.0681 72  10.803  <.0001
 Baseline - 12 Months    1.036 0.0681 72  15.207  <.0001
 3 Months - 6 Months     0.320 0.0681 72   4.697  0.0001
 3 Months - 12 Months    0.620 0.0681 72   9.101  <.0001
 6 Months - 12 Months    0.300 0.0681 72   4.404  0.0002

P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 4 estimates 



Interpreting Post-Hoc Results
The emmeans output shows pairwise comparisons for all time point combinations. Significant values (p.value < 0.05) indicate that those time points have significantly different mean HbA1c levels.
How to read the output:
First section (emmeans):

Shows estimated marginal mean HbA1c at each time point
Includes standard error (SE) and confidence intervals

Second section (pairwise comparisons):

contrast: Which two time points are being compared
estimate: Difference between the two time point means
SE: Standard error of the difference
df: Degrees of freedom
t.ratio: Test statistic
p.value: Adjusted p-value (controlling for multiple comparisons)

section: Example 2: Staff Burnout Across Shift Schedules
text:
Example 2: Staff Burnout Across Shift Schedules
A hospital HR department wants to study nurse burnout using the Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI) emotional exhaustion subscale (score range: 0-54). They measure the same 20 nurses under three different shift schedules:

Schedule A: Traditional 8-hour shifts
Schedule B: 12-hour shifts
Schedule C: Flexible self-scheduling

Multiple studies have examined the relationship between shift hours and nurse burnout, with research across multiple countries and care settings showing significant associations between shift length and burnout levels.
Each nurse works under each schedule for one month, with washout periods between.

# Burnout scores for 20 nurses under 3 shift schedules
n_nurses <- 20

schedule_A <- c(32, 35, 28, 38, 30, 36, 33, 29, 37, 31,
                34, 27, 39, 32, 35, 30, 36, 28, 34, 31)

schedule_B <- c(38, 42, 35, 44, 37, 41, 39, 36, 43, 38,
                40, 34, 45, 39, 42, 37, 43, 35, 41, 38)

schedule_C <- c(25, 28, 22, 30, 24, 29, 26, 23, 31, 25,
                27, 21, 32, 26, 29, 24, 30, 22, 28, 25)

# Create data frame
burnout_data <- data.frame(
  nurse_id = rep(1:n_nurses, 3),
  schedule = factor(rep(c("A: 8-hour", "B: 12-hour", "C: Flexible"),
                        each = n_nurses)),
  burnout = c(schedule_A, schedule_B, schedule_C)
)











# Repeated-measures ANOVA
rm_anova_burnout <- aov(burnout ~ schedule + Error(nurse_id/schedule),
                        data = burnout_data)
summary(rm_anova_burnout)


Error: nurse_id
          Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
Residuals  1 0.1906  0.1906               

Error: nurse_id:schedule
         Df Sum Sq Mean Sq
schedule  2   1290   645.3

Error: Within
          Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
schedule   2  400.7  200.34    17.4 1.47e-06 ***
Residuals 54  621.6   11.51                     
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

# Post-hoc tests
emm_schedule <- emmeans(rm_anova_burnout, ~ schedule)
pairs(emm_schedule, adjust = "tukey")

 contrast                   estimate   SE df t.ratio p.value
 (A: 8-hour) - (B: 12-hour)    -6.17 2.23 54  -2.770  0.0206
 (A: 8-hour) - C: Flexible      6.97 2.23 54   3.126  0.0079
 (B: 12-hour) - C: Flexible    13.14 2.23 54   5.896  <.0001

P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 3 estimates 



Interpretation
The highly significant F-test indicates that burnout levels differ across shift schedules.
Post-hoc tests reveal that:

Flexible scheduling (C) results in significantly lower burnout than both traditional (A) and 12-hour (B) shifts
12-hour shifts (B) result in significantly higher burnout than 8-hour shifts (A)

This has important implications for nurse retention and patient safety.

section: Why ANOVA Matters for Healthcare Managers
text:
Why ANOVA Matters for Healthcare Managers

One-way ANOVA enables evidence-based comparisons across multiple departments, facilities, treatment protocols, or patient populations simultaneously while controlling Type I error.
Repeated-measures ANOVA is essential for evaluating longitudinal programs and interventions, tracking patient outcomes over time, measuring the effectiveness of quality improvement initiatives, or assessing staff development programs.
Post-hoc tests ensure that when you identify “significant differences,” you can understand exactly where those differences lie, enabling targeted action rather than broad, unfocused interventions.

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
In ANOVA, the term “way” refers to the number of independent variables (or factors) we are examining:

One-Way ANOVA: Analyzes the effect of one factor on an outcome

Example: Does patient satisfaction differ across 4 hospital departments?
Factor: Department (4 levels: Emergency, Cardiology, Orthopedics, Oncology)
Outcome: Satisfaction score

Two-Way ANOVA: Analyzes the effects of two factors simultaneously on an outcome

Example: Does pain reduction depend on both treatment type AND disease severity?
Factor A: Treatment (2 levels: Standard, New)
Factor B: Severity (3 levels: Mild, Moderate, Severe)
Outcome: Pain reduction score






In healthcare settings, outcomes are rarely influenced by a single factor.
For example, the effectiveness of an intervention type (e.g., standard vs. intensive care) can vary depending on disease severity (e.g., mild, moderate, severe).
While one-way ANOVA can only examine one factor at a time, two-way ANOVA allows us to understand if the effect of one factor depends on the level of another factor. This is called an interaction effect, and it’s one of the most important concepts in healthcare research.
Two-way ANOVA allows us to:

Test the effect of Factor A (main effect of A, e.g., intervention type)
Test the effect of Factor B (main effect of B, e.g., disease severity)
Test whether the effect of A depends on B (interaction effect A × B, e.g., intervention type × disease severity)






A main effect is the overall effect of one factor, averaging across all levels of the other factor.

Main effect of Treatment: Does the treatment affect outcomes, regardless of patient group?
Main effect of Patient Group: Do patient groups differ in outcomes, regardless of treatment?




An interaction effect occurs when the effect of one factor depends on the level of another factor.

The new drug works well for younger patients but not for older patients
The training program improves performance for novice nurses (work experience < 2 years) but not experienced nurses (work experience > 2 years)

When an interaction is present, main effects can be misleading! If a drug helps one group but harms another, the “average” effect might be zero.

Factor B
Example

Within-Subjects
Same subjects

Drug type × Time of day
