title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Visualizing Interactions
The easiest way to understand interactions is through interaction plots, where we plot means for each combination of factors. The pattern of lines tells us about the interaction.

Pattern 1: Parallel Lines (No Interaction)
When there is no interaction, the effect of one factor is the same across all levels of the other factor. The lines in the interaction plot are parallel.









Interpretation: The new treatment improves outcomes by 15 points for both mild and severe patients. The treatment effect is consistent regardless of severity.


Pattern 2: Ordinal Interaction (Converging/Diverging Lines)
In an ordinal interaction, the lines converge or diverge but do not cross. The effect of one factor is larger at some levels of the other factor, but the direction is the same.









Interpretation: The new treatment helps both groups, but it helps severe patients much more (+25 points) than mild patients (+10 points). The treatment is beneficial for everyone, but especially for those with severe disease.


Pattern 3: Disordinal (Crossover) Interaction
In a disordinal (or crossover) interaction, the lines cross. The effect of one factor reverses direction at different levels of the other factor.









Interpretation: The new treatment helps severe patients (+30 points) but harms mild patients (-10 points). The main effect of treatment might appear small or non-significant because the positive and negative effects cancel out.

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Why Interactions Matter in Healthcare
Understanding interactions is important in healthcare management because:

Personalized medicine: Treatment effectiveness often varies by patient characteristics
Resource allocation: Interventions may work better in some settings or groups than others
Safety: A treatment safe for one population may be harmful for another
Policy decisions: Program effectiveness may depend on implementation context

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
What is it?
A two-way between-subjects ANOVA tests the effects of two independent variables (factors) on a continuous dependent variable, where different participants are in each combination of factor levels.

Key Components

Two factors (each with 2 or more levels)
Each participant is in only one cell of the design
Tests three effects: Main effect A, Main effect B, A × B interaction

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
When to Use It

Comparing the effectiveness of treatment types (e.g., medication A vs. B vs. C) across patient demographics (e.g., age groups, gender, comorbidity status)
Evaluating interventions (e.g., discharge planning programs: telehealth vs. in-person care) across facility types (e.g., academic medical centers, community hospitals, rural critical access hospitals)
Assessing programs (e.g., traditional lecture, simulation-based, blended learning) across staff experience levels (e.g., novice, intermediate, expert nurses)

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Scenario 1: Treatment × Disease Severity
Let’s think about the following case:
A clinical trial compares two treatments (Standard vs. Novel) for chronic pain across three severity levels (Mild, Moderate, Severe). The outcome is pain reduction score (0-100, higher = better).
Research on chronic pain management has shown that treatment effectiveness often varies by baseline disease severity and patient phenotype. Understanding these interactions is critical for personalized pain management approaches.
Research questions:

Does the novel treatment reduce pain more than standard care (main effect of treatment)?
Does pain reduction vary by baseline severity (the main effect of severity levels)?
Does the treatment effect depend on severity (interaction)?

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
The Formula
Two-way ANOVA partitions variance into four components:
\[SS_{total} = SS_A + SS_B + SS_{A \times B} + SS_{error}\]
Three F-statistics are calculated:
\[F_A = \frac{MS_A}{MS_{error}}, \quad F_B = \frac{MS_B}{MS_{error}}, \quad F_{A \times B} = \frac{MS_{A \times B}}{MS_{error}}\]
The degrees of freedom:

Factor A: \(df_A = a - 1\)
Factor B: \(df_B = b - 1\)
Interaction: \(df_{A \times B} = (a-1)(b-1)\)
Error: \(df_{error} = N - ab\)

Where

\(a\) = levels of A
\(b\) = levels of B
\(N\) = total sample size.

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Example: Treatment × Disease Severity
Let’s create a dataset and examine summary statistics.

# Pain reduction scores for 2 treatments × 3 severity levels
# 15 patients per cell = 90 total
n_per_cell <- 15

# Generate data with interaction effect
# Novel treatment works better for severe patients
set.seed(2026)

pain_data <- expand.grid(
  treatment = c("Standard", "Novel"),
  severity = c("Mild", "Moderate", "Severe"),
  subject = 1:n_per_cell
) %>%
  mutate(
    # Base effect of severity (less reduction for more severe)
    base = case_when(
      severity == "Mild" ~ 70,
      severity == "Moderate" ~ 55,
      severity == "Severe" ~ 40
    ),
    # Treatment effect varies by severity (interaction)
    treatment_effect = case_when(
      treatment == "Standard" ~ 0,
      treatment == "Novel" & severity == "Mild" ~ 5,
      treatment == "Novel" & severity == "Moderate" ~ 12,
      treatment == "Novel" & severity == "Severe" ~ 22
    ),
    # Add random error
    pain_reduction = base + treatment_effect + rnorm(n(), 0, 6)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    severity = factor(severity, levels = c("Mild", "Moderate", "Severe")),
    treatment = factor(treatment, levels = c("Standard", "Novel"))
  )

Conducting Two-Way Between-Subjects ANOVA in R

# Two-way ANOVA
anova_pain <- aov(pain_reduction ~ treatment * severity, data = pain_data)
summary(anova_pain)

treatment           1   5053    5053  140.65  < 2e-16 ***
severity            2   6736    3368   93.74  < 2e-16 ***

Residuals          84   3018      36

Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1



Interpreting the ANOVA Table
The output shows three tests:

treatment: Main effect of treatment (averaging across severity levels)
severity: Main effect of severity (averaging across treatments)
treatment:severity: Interaction effect

Results interpretation:

Main effect of treatment: Significant main effect of treatment on average (pain reduction differs across treatments)
Main effect of severity: Significant main effect of severity (pain reduction differs across severity levels)
Interaction: Significant treatment X severity interaction (the treatment effect differs depending on severity level)



When Interaction is Significant

Do not interpret main effects in isolation when the interaction is significant!
The significant interaction tells us that the novel treatment’s benefit varies by severity. To understand this pattern, we need to examine simple effects.

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Simple Effects Analysis (post-hoc analysis)
Simple effects examine the effect of one factor at each level of the other factor. We use the emmeans package for this analysis.

# Get estimated marginal means
emm <- emmeans(anova_pain, ~ treatment | severity)

# Simple effects: treatment effect at each severity level
pairs(emm, adjust = "tukey")

severity = Mild:
 contrast         estimate   SE df t.ratio p.value

severity = Moderate:

severity = Severe:
 contrast         estimate   SE df t.ratio p.value
 Standard - Novel   -23.51 2.19 84 -10.740  <.0001



Interpreting Simple Effects
This shows the treatment effect (Standard - Novel) at each severity level:

Mild: Significant difference (Novel > Standard)
Moderate: Significant difference (Novel > Standard)
Severe: Significant difference (Novel > Standard)

The novel treatment provides the greatest benefit for patients at all disease severity levels.

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Example 2: Training Method × Experience Level
A hospital evaluates two training methods (Lecture vs. Simulation) for medication safety competency across three experience levels (Novice: <1 year, Intermediate: 1-5 years, Expert: >5 years).
Research comparing training approaches has demonstrated that simulation-based education is particularly effective for novice nurses, while the benefits may vary by experience level.
Let’s create a dataset.

# Generate data with crossover interaction
n_cell <- 12

training_data <- expand.grid(
  method = c("Lecture", "Simulation"),
  experience = c("Novice", "Intermediate", "Expert"),
  subject = 1:n_cell
) %>%
  mutate(
    # Crossover interaction: simulation helps novices but lecture helps experts
    score = case_when(
      method == "Lecture" & experience == "Novice" ~ 68,
      method == "Lecture" & experience == "Intermediate" ~ 78,
      method == "Lecture" & experience == "Expert" ~ 88,
      method == "Simulation" & experience == "Novice" ~ 82,
      method == "Simulation" & experience == "Intermediate" ~ 80,
      method == "Simulation" & experience == "Expert" ~ 79
    ) + rnorm(n(), 0, 4),
    experience = factor(experience, levels = c("Novice", "Intermediate", "Expert"))
  )











# Two-way ANOVA
anova_training <- aov(score ~ method * experience, data = training_data)

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Practice Activity 1: Intervention × Facility Type
A health system evaluates the effect of care transition program on readmission rates (30-days readmission rate in %) across facility types. Analyze whether the intervention effect depends on facility type.
Care Transition Programs help patients move safely from hospital to home, reducing probability of readmission:

Standard Discharge: Basic discharge instructions, prescription reconciliation, follow-up appointment scheduled
Enhanced Transition Program: Includes all standard elements + dedicated transition coordinator, post-discharge phone call within 48 hours, home medication review, connection to community resources

Facility Types differ in resources, patient populations, and care complexity:

Urban Academic Medical Centers: Large teaching hospitals treating complex cases, with many specialists, electronic health systems, and dedicated staff for care coordination
Suburban Community Hospitals: Mid-sized hospitals serving local communities with standard medical services and moderate staffing levels
Rural Critical Access Hospitals: Small hospitals (<25 beds) in remote areas with limited specialists and support staff; patients often travel long distances for care

Studies have found that enhanced transition programs reduce readmissions more effectively in some settings than others. Academic medical centers, which already have baseline infrastructure and care coordinators, may see smaller improvements from adding enhanced programs compared to their standard discharge processes. In contrast, rural hospitals, which often lack dedicated transition staff, may experience larger reductions in readmissions when enhanced programs are implemented, despite having fewer overall resources. Community hospitals typically fall between these two extremes. These differences suggest that “one-size-fits-all” transition programs may not be the most cost-effective approach across diverse facility types.

# 30-day readmission rates (%)
n_cell <- 10
set.seed(2006)

intervention_data <- expand.grid(
  program = c("Standard Discharge", "Enhanced Transition"),
  facility = c("Urban Academic", "Suburban Community", "Rural Critical Access"),
  id = 1:n_cell
) %>%
  mutate(
    readmit_rate = case_when(
      program == "Standard Discharge" & facility == "Urban Academic" ~ 14,
      program == "Standard Discharge" & facility == "Suburban Community" ~ 12,
      program == "Standard Discharge" & facility == "Rural Critical Access" ~ 16,
      program == "Enhanced Transition" & facility == "Urban Academic" ~ 13,
      program == "Enhanced Transition" & facility == "Suburban Community" ~ 9,
      program == "Enhanced Transition" & facility == "Rural Critical Access" ~ 8
    ) + rnorm(n(), 0, 1.5)
  )

# Your code here:
# 1. Create an interaction plot
# 2. Run two-way ANOVA
# 3. Conduct simple effects analysis if interaction is significant
# 4. Interpret the results for healthcare administrators



Code
# Solution
anova_int <- aov(readmit_rate ~ program * facility, data = intervention_data)
summary(anova_int)
emmeans(anova_int, ~ program | facility) %>% pairs(adjust = "tukey")

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Practice Activity 2: Medication × Age Group
A healthcare system compares the effectiveness of two pain medications across three age groups to inform formulary decisions and prescribing guidelines.
Context:
Pain Medications represent different treatment options:

Drug A: Standard anti-inflammatory medication
Drug B: Combination medication targeting multiple pain pathways

Age Groups differ in how their bodies process medications and respond to treatment:

Young Adults (18-40): Bodies process drugs quickly, generally have fewer other health conditions
Middle-Aged (41-65): Bodies process drugs more slowly than younger adults, more likely to have conditions like high blood pressure or diabetes
Older Adults (65+): Bodies process drugs most slowly, often take multiple medications, higher risk of drug side effects and interactions

Outcome Variable: Pain relief score (0-100 scale, higher scores = better pain control)
What Research Has Shown:
Clinical studies have found that combination pain medications (Drug B) may work differently across age groups. In younger patients, combination drugs often provide only modest improvements over standard medications, possibly because their bodies process drugs efficiently regardless of the drug type. However, in older patients, combination medications that work through multiple pathways have shown significantly better pain relief compared to standard single-mechanism drugs. This may be because older adults’ bodies respond better when pain is targeted from multiple angles simultaneously. Middle-aged patients typically show intermediate responses. Understanding these age-related patterns helps hospitals make evidence-based decisions about which medications to stock and prescribe for different patient populations.

n_cell <- 15

medication_data <- expand.grid(
  medication = c("Drug A", "Drug B"),
  age_group = c("Young (18-40)", "Middle (41-65)", "Older (65+)"),
  patient = 1:n_cell
) %>%
  mutate(
    # Ordinal interaction
    pain_relief = case_when(
      medication == "Drug A" ~ 55 + rnorm(n(), 0, 6),
      medication == "Drug B" & age_group == "Young (18-40)" ~ 58 + rnorm(n(), 0, 6),
      medication == "Drug B" & age_group == "Middle (41-65)" ~ 68 + rnorm(n(), 0, 6),
      medication == "Drug B" & age_group == "Older (65+)" ~ 78 + rnorm(n(), 0, 6)
    )
  )

# Your code here:



Code
# Solution
anova_med <- aov(pain_relief ~ medication * age_group, data = medication_data)
summary(anova_med)
emmeans(anova_med, ~ medication | age_group) %>% pairs(adjust = "tukey")

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
What is it?
A two-way within-subjects ANOVA (also called two-way repeated-measures ANOVA) tests the effects of two factors where the same participants experience all combinations of both factors.

Key Characteristics

Same participants measured under all conditions
Both factors are within-subjects (repeated measures)
More powerful than between-subjects designs (controls for individual differences)
Requires fewer participants

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
When to Use It
Use two-way within-subjects ANOVA when the same participants are measured under all combinations of two factors:

Same patients tested with different medications (e.g., Drug A, Drug B, Drug C) at different times of day (e.g., morning, evening)
Same staff evaluated on multiple tasks (e.g., vital signs, medication administration, charting) across multiple assessment periods (e.g., pre-training, post-training, 3-month follow-up)
Same clinics measured on different metrics (e.g., patient satisfaction, wait time, quality scores) in different seasons (e.g., winter, spring, summer, fall)

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
section: Scenario: Medication Type × Time of Day
text:
Scenario: Medication Type × Time of Day
A clinical study examines whether medication effectiveness varies by time of administration. The same 20 patients receive each of three medications at two different times (morning and evening), with appropriate rest periods between medications.
Study Design:
This is a within-subjects design where each patient tries all medication and time combinations:

Each patient receives Med A in the morning, Med A in the evening
Each patient receives Med B in the morning, Med B in the evening
Each patient receives Med C in the morning, Med C in the evening
Total: 6 conditions per patient (3 medications × 2 times)
Rest periods (washout periods) are included between medications to ensure one drug doesn’t affect the next

Medications Being Tested:

Med A: Standard pain reliever
Med B: Extended-release pain medication
Med C: Fast-acting pain medication

Outcome Variable: Medication effectiveness score (0-100, higher = better pain control)
Research has found that medication timing can significantly affect pain relief. Studies show that some pain medications work better when taken in the evening, providing longer pain relief with fewer side effects, while others may be more effective in the morning. Understanding these timing patterns helps doctors make better prescribing recommendations, potentially improving patient outcomes without increasing medication doses.
Let’s create a dataset

# Same 20 patients, all conditions
set.seed(2026)
n_patients <- 20

# Generate data
within_data <- expand.grid(
  patient_id = 1:n_patients,
  medication = c("Med A", "Med B", "Med C"),
  time = c("Morning", "Evening")
) %>%
  mutate(
    # Patient random effect
    patient_effect = rep(rnorm(n_patients, 0, 5), 6),
    # Fixed effects with interaction
    # Med A (standard): works better in evening (like NSAIDs in research)
    # Med B (extended-release): similar effectiveness both times
    # Med C (fast-acting): works better in morning when body is active
    fixed = case_when(
      medication == "Med A" & time == "Morning" ~ 63,
      medication == "Med A" & time == "Evening" ~ 72,
      medication == "Med B" & time == "Morning" ~ 70,
      medication == "Med B" & time == "Evening" ~ 71,
      medication == "Med C" & time == "Morning" ~ 77,
      medication == "Med C" & time == "Evening" ~ 65
    ),
    effectiveness = fixed + patient_effect + rnorm(n(), 0, 3)
  )

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
section: Practice Activity 3: Task Type × Shift Period
text:
Practice Activity 3: Task Type × Shift Period
A hospital nursing director evaluates whether nurse performance on different task types changes throughout a shift. The same 15 nurses are evaluated on two task types across three shift periods.
Study Design:
This is a within-subjects design where each nurse is evaluated under all task-period combinations:

Each nurse performs documentation tasks at the beginning, middle, and end of shift
Each nurse performs patient care tasks at the beginning, middle, and end of shift
Total: 6 evaluations per nurse (2 task types × 3 shift periods)

Task Types:

Documentation: Completing patient charts, entering data into electronic health records, processing admission/discharge paperwork
Patient Care: Direct patient interactions including vital signs monitoring, medication administration, patient education, responding to patient needs

Shift Periods:

Beginning: First 2-3 hours of 12-hour shift (nurses are fresh but orientation to patients is ongoing)
Middle: Hours 4-8 of shift (nurses are familiar with patients, workload is often highest)
End: Final 2-3 hours of shift (fatigue may set in, handoff preparation begins)

Outcome Variable: Performance score (0-100, based on supervisor observation, higher = better performance)
Understanding how different tasks are affected by shift fatigue helps hospital administrators make evidence-based staffing and workflow decisions. For example, if documentation quality declines significantly toward the end of shifts while patient care remains stable, managers might schedule additional clerical support during late shift hours or redesign workflows to complete complex documentation earlier in shifts. This can improve both staff well-being and patient safety.

n_nurses <- 15

task_data <- expand.grid(
  nurse_id = 1:n_nurses,
  task = c("Documentation", "Patient Care"),
  period = c("Beginning", "Middle", "End")
) %>%
  mutate(
    nurse_effect = rep(rnorm(n_nurses, 0, 4), 6),
    # Performance declines more for documentation than patient care
    fixed = case_when(
      task == "Documentation" & period == "Beginning" ~ 90,
      task == "Documentation" & period == "Middle" ~ 82,
      task == "Documentation" & period == "End" ~ 70,
      task == "Patient Care" & period == "Beginning" ~ 88,
      task == "Patient Care" & period == "Middle" ~ 85,
      task == "Patient Care" & period == "End" ~ 80
    ),
    performance = fixed + nurse_effect + rnorm(n(), 0, 3),
    period = factor(period, levels = c("Beginning", "Middle", "End"))
  )

# Your code here:
# 1. Create interaction plot
# 2. Run two-way within-subjects ANOVA
# 3. Interpret the interaction



Code
# Solution
task_anova <- aov(performance ~ task * period + Error(nurse_id/(task * period)),
                  data = task_data)
summary(task_anova)
emmeans(task_anova, ~ task | period) %>% pairs(adjust = "tukey")

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
What is it?
A mixed design ANOVA combines both between-subjects and within-subjects factors. This is one of the most common designs in healthcare research.

Key Characteristics

One or more between-subjects factors: Different participants in each group
One or more within-subjects factors: Same participants measured repeatedly
Tests main effects of both factor types and their interaction

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
When to Use It
Use mixed design ANOVA when different groups of participants are measured repeatedly over time:

Clinical trials: Treatment group (e.g., new drug, standard drug, placebo) × Time points (e.g., baseline, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months)
Training studies: Program type (e.g., online learning, in-person workshop, blended approach) × Assessment occasions (e.g., before training, immediately after, 1-month follow-up, 3-month follow-up)
Quality improvement: Intervention group (e.g., standard care, enhanced protocol) × Measurement periods (e.g., before intervention, 3 months after, 6 months after, 12 months after)

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Scenario: Training Program × Assessment Time
Let’s think about the following case:
A hospital compares three training programs for improving nursing competency. Nurses are randomly assigned to one program (between-subjects factor) and assessed at three time points (within-subjects factor): Before training, Immediately after training, and 3 months later.
Study Design:
This is a mixed design where different nurses are assigned to different programs (between-subjects), but each nurse is tested multiple times (within-subjects):

60 nurses total (20 assigned to each program)
Each nurse is tested 3 times: before training, right after training, 3 months later
The question: Do different training programs show different patterns of learning and retention over time?

Training Programs:

Traditional Lecture: Classroom instruction with PowerPoint presentations, lectures, and written materials. Lower cost, can train many nurses at once.
Simulation-Based: Hands-on practice with medical mannequins and equipment in a simulated hospital environment. Higher cost, smaller class sizes, allows practicing skills safely.
Blended Learning: Combination of online modules for theory (completed at own pace) plus in-person skill practice sessions. Moderate cost, flexible scheduling.

Outcome Variable: Competency test score (0-100, covering both knowledge and skills, higher scores = higher competencies)
Studies comparing nursing training methods have found that simulation-based and blended learning approaches generally produce better learning outcomes than traditional lecture-only methods, with students scoring higher on competency tests. However, the key management question is about long-term retention: Do more expensive training methods maintain their advantage over time, or do all methods “fade” equally? Research shows that hands-on training methods (simulation and blended) show better long-term retention compared to lecture-only approaches. Understanding these patterns helps hospitals justify the higher upfront costs of simulation or blended programs if they provide lasting benefits.

n_per_group <- 20

mixed_data <- expand.grid(
  nurse_id = 1:(n_per_group * 3),
  time = c("Pre", "Post", "3 Months")
) %>%
  mutate(
    # Assign to groups
    program = rep(rep(c("Traditional", "Simulation", "Blended"),
                      each = n_per_group), 3),
    # Nurse random effect
    nurse_effect = rep(rnorm(n_per_group * 3, 0, 4), 3),
    # Fixed effects
    fixed = case_when(
      # Traditional: modest improvement, significant decay
      program == "Traditional" & time == "Pre" ~ 65,
      program == "Traditional" & time == "Post" ~ 75,
      program == "Traditional" & time == "3 Months" ~ 66,
      # Simulation: good improvement, well maintained
      program == "Simulation" & time == "Pre" ~ 65,
      program == "Simulation" & time == "Post" ~ 84,
      program == "Simulation" & time == "3 Months" ~ 79,
      # Blended: best improvement, well maintained
      program == "Blended" & time == "Pre" ~ 65,
      program == "Blended" & time == "Post" ~ 88,
      program == "Blended" & time == "3 Months" ~ 85
    ),
    score = fixed + nurse_effect + rnorm(n(), 0, 3),
    time = factor(time, levels = c("Pre", "Post", "3 Months"))
  )

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Example 2: Intervention Group × Measurement Occasions
A diabetes clinic evaluates the effectiveness of an intensive education program. Patients with Type 2 diabetes are randomly assigned to two groups (between-subjects factor) and their blood sugar control is measured at three time points (within-subjects factor): Baseline, 3 months, and 6 months.
Study Design:
This is a mixed design where different patients are assigned to different programs (between-subjects), but each patient is measured multiple times (within-subjects):

50 patients total (25 assigned to each group)
Each patient’s HbA1c is tested 3 times: at the start, after 3 months, after 6 months
The question: Does the intensive education program produce better blood sugar control over time compared to usual care?

Intervention Groups:

Usual Care: Standard diabetes management with quarterly doctor visits, basic diet and medication instructions. Typical approach used in most clinics.
Intensive Education: Includes everything in usual care + weekly group classes covering diet planning, carbohydrate counting, exercise strategies, medication management, and blood glucose monitoring. Also includes individual counseling sessions and continuous glucose monitoring with feedback.

Outcome Variable: HbA1c level (%)
HbA1c (Hemoglobin A1c) is a blood test that shows average blood sugar control over the past 2-3 months. It measures the percentage of hemoglobin (a protein in red blood cells) that has sugar attached to it. The higher the percentage, the poorer the blood sugar control. Lower numbers are better:

Below 7.0%: Good control (target for most diabetes patients)
7.0-8.0%: Moderate control
Above 8.0%: Poor control, higher risk of complications

Research has shown that intensive diabetes education programs can significantly improve blood sugar control. Studies typically find that patients in intensive programs show greater HbA1c reductions compared to usual care, with benefits becoming more pronounced over time as patients apply what they’ve learned. Understanding whether these programs produce sustained improvements (or if effects fade) helps hospitals decide whether to invest in comprehensive education programs versus standard approaches.
Let’s create a dataset using the following code:

n_group <- 25

diabetes_mixed <- expand.grid(
  patient_id = 1:(n_group * 2),
  time = c("Baseline", "3 Months", "6 Months")
) %>%
  mutate(
    group = rep(rep(c("Usual Care", "Intensive Education"), each = n_group), 3),
    patient_effect = rep(rnorm(n_group * 2, 0, 0.5), 3),
    fixed = case_when(
      group == "Usual Care" & time == "Baseline" ~ 8.5,
      group == "Usual Care" & time == "3 Months" ~ 8.3,
      group == "Usual Care" & time == "6 Months" ~ 8.2,
      group == "Intensive Education" & time == "Baseline" ~ 8.5,
      group == "Intensive Education" & time == "3 Months" ~ 8.0,
      group == "Intensive Education" & time == "6 Months" ~ 7.1
    ),
    hba1c = fixed + patient_effect + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.3),
    time = factor(time, levels = c("Baseline", "3 Months", "6 Months"))
  )











# Mixed ANOVA
diabetes_anova <- aov(hba1c ~ group * time + Error(patient_id/time),
                      data = diabetes_mixed)
summary(diabetes_anova)

section: Practice Activity 4: Therapy Type × Session Number
text:
Practice Activity 4: Therapy Type × Session Number
A mental health clinic compares the effectiveness of two therapy approaches for treating anxiety. Patients are randomly assigned to one therapy type (between-subjects factor) and their anxiety levels are measured at three time points (within-subjects factor).
Study Design:
This is a mixed design where different patients receive different therapies (between-subjects), but each patient is measured multiple times (within-subjects):

36 patients total (18 assigned to each therapy type)
Each patient’s anxiety is measured at 3 time points: Session 1 (baseline), Session 3 (mid-treatment), Session 5 (end of treatment)
The question: Do CBT and Mindfulness show different patterns of anxiety reduction over the treatment period?

Therapy Approaches:

CBT (Cognitive Behavioral Therapy): Focuses on identifying and changing negative thought patterns and behaviors. Therapist works with patient to challenge anxious thoughts and practice new coping behaviors. Often includes homework assignments between sessions.
Mindfulness-Based Therapy: Focuses on present-moment awareness and acceptance of thoughts and feelings without judgment. Includes meditation practices, breathing exercises, and body awareness techniques. Emphasizes observing anxiety without trying to change it.

Outcome Variable: Anxiety score (0-100, higher scores = more severe anxiety symptoms)
Research comparing CBT and mindfulness-based therapies has found that while both approaches effectively reduce anxiety, they may show different improvement patterns over time. Some studies suggest CBT produces faster initial symptom reduction because it directly targets anxious thoughts and behaviors from the first session. Mindfulness-based approaches may show more gradual improvement as patients build meditation skills and learn to respond differently to anxiety. Understanding these different trajectories helps clinicians make informed recommendations about which therapy might be best for patients with different needs (e.g., those needing rapid relief vs. those interested in long-term coping skills).

n_group <- 18

therapy_data <- expand.grid(
  patient_id = 1:(n_group * 2),
  session = c("Session 1", "Session 3", "Session 5")
) %>%
  mutate(
    therapy = rep(rep(c("CBT", "Mindfulness"), each = n_group), 3),
    patient_effect = rep(rnorm(n_group * 2, 0, 4), 3),
    # CBT shows faster initial improvement; Mindfulness catches up
    fixed = case_when(
      therapy == "CBT" & session == "Session 1" ~ 65,
      therapy == "CBT" & session == "Session 3" ~ 48,
      therapy == "CBT" & session == "Session 5" ~ 42,
      therapy == "Mindfulness" & session == "Session 1" ~ 65,
      therapy == "Mindfulness" & session == "Session 3" ~ 55,
      therapy == "Mindfulness" & session == "Session 5" ~ 40
    ),
    anxiety = fixed + patient_effect + rnorm(n(), 0, 3),
    session = factor(session, levels = c("Session 1", "Session 3", "Session 5"))
  )

# Your code here:
# 1. Create interaction plot
# 2. Run mixed design ANOVA
# 3. Conduct simple effects analysis
# 4. What would you tell patients about choosing between therapies?



Code
# Solution
therapy_anova <- aov(anxiety ~ therapy * session + Error(patient_id/session),
                     data = therapy_data)
summary(therapy_anova)
emmeans(therapy_anova, ~ therapy | session) %>% pairs(adjust = "tukey")

title: ANOVA 2: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Practice Activity 5: Facility Type × Time
A health system implements a patient safety improvement initiative and tracks progress across three facility types (between-subjects factor) at two time points (within-subjects factor).
Study Design:
This is a mixed design where different facilities have different characteristics (between-subjects), but each facility is measured multiple times (within-subjects):

45 facilities total (15 of each type)
Each facility’s safety score is measured at 2 time points: Baseline (before initiative) and 6 Months (after implementing initiative)
The question: Do different facility types show different rates of safety improvement?

Facility Types:

Urban Hospitals: Large hospitals in cities with high patient volumes, diverse patient populations, extensive resources, and specialized safety teams. Typically already have strong baseline safety infrastructure.
Suburban Hospitals: Mid-sized hospitals in suburban areas with moderate patient volumes and resources. Often have established quality improvement programs but fewer specialized staff than urban centers.
Rural Hospitals: Small hospitals in remote areas with limited resources, smaller safety teams, and fewer quality improvement staff. May have lower baseline safety scores but greater potential for improvement.

Outcome Variable: Patient safety score (0-100, based on incident reporting, medication errors, infection rates, and safety protocols compliance)
Research on quality improvement initiatives shows that different facility types often demonstrate different improvement trajectories. Rural hospitals, despite having lower baseline scores, may show steeper improvement rates when given new resources and training because they’re implementing systematic safety practices for the first time. Urban hospitals may show slower improvement rates because they already have strong safety programs in place (ceiling effect). Understanding these different patterns helps health system administrators allocate quality improvement resources effectively and set realistic improvement targets for different facility types.

n_facilities <- 15

safety_data <- expand.grid(
  facility_id = 1:(n_facilities * 3),
  time = c("Baseline", "6 Months")
) %>%
  mutate(
    type = rep(rep(c("Urban", "Suburban", "Rural"), each = n_facilities), 2),
    facility_effect = rep(rnorm(n_facilities * 3, 0, 3), 2),
    fixed = case_when(
      type == "Urban" & time == "Baseline" ~ 80,
      type == "Urban" & time == "6 Months" ~ 85,
      type == "Suburban" & time == "Baseline" ~ 78,
      type == "Suburban" & time == "6 Months" ~ 86,
      type == "Rural" & time == "Baseline" ~ 68,
      type == "Rural" & time == "6 Months" ~ 84
    ),
    score = fixed + facility_effect + rnorm(n(), 0, 2),
    time = factor(time, levels = c("Baseline", "6 Months"))
  )

# Your code here:



Code
# Solution
safety_anova <- aov(score ~ type * time + Error(facility_id/time),
                    data = safety_data)
summary(safety_anova)
emmeans(safety_anova, ~ type | time) %>% pairs(adjust = "tukey")

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
t-tests are among the most fundamental and widely-used statistical tools that allow us to make data-driven decisions by comparing means and determining whether observed differences are simply due to chance or not.
Consider this scenario: A hospital administrator notices that their emergency department’s average waiting time appears to be 52 minutes, while the regional standard is 45 minutes. Is this 7-minute difference a systematic problem that needs addressing, or could it simply be random variation in the data? This is exactly the type of question that t-tests help us answer.
t-tests determine whether observed differences are statistically significant. In other words, they examine whether the differences we see in our sample data likely reflect true differences in the population, or whether they could have occurred simply by chance. This distinction is critical because acting on random noise can waste resources, while ignoring real problems can harm outcomes.



There are three types of t-tests, each designed for different research scenarios:








Test Type
Purpose
Example




One-sample
Compare a sample mean to a known or hypothesized value
Testing if average wait time differs from a 45-minute standard


Independent-samples
Compare means from two separate, unrelated groups
Comparing processing times between two different intake systems


Paired-samples
Compare two related measurements on the same subjects
Measuring scores before and after an intervention



Understanding when to use each type is crucial for valid statistical inference. Using the wrong test can lead to incorrect conclusions (i.e., either finding differences that don’t exist or missing differences that do). The following sections will explain each test in detail, with worked examples and R code that you can apply to your own data.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
What is it?
A one-sample t-test is a statistical procedure that compares a sample mean to a known or hypothesized population value. It answers a fundamental question: Is our sample mean significantly different from a specific benchmark, or could the difference we observe be due to random chance?
This test is particularly useful when you have a single group of observations and want to compare their average to some external standard or target value. For example, if there is a law regarding a maximum acceptable waiting time, or if industry benchmarks establish expected performance levels, the one-sample t-test helps you determine whether your organization is meeting those standards.

Key Components

One group of observations (your sample data)
One comparison value (a benchmark, standard, target, or known or hypothesized mean)

The test works by calculating how far your sample mean deviates from the comparison value, relative to the variability in your data. If this deviation is large enough, we conclude that the difference is unlikely to have occurred by chance alone.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
When to Use It
The one-sample t-test is appropriate whenever you need to compare your data against a fixed reference point. Common scenarios include:

Comparing performance against national or industry benchmarks (e.g., average length of stay compared to national average)
Testing if outcomes meet target levels set by management or regulators (e.g., patient satisfaction scores vs. a target of 8.0)
Evaluating if measurements achieve recommended standards (e.g., medication dosages achieving target blood levels)
Assessing if operational metrics meet regulatory requirements (e.g., waiting times vs. regulatory standards)

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
Scenario: Emergency Department Waiting Times
Imagine you are an administrator at a hospital where the regional average emergency department waiting time is 45 minutes. Recently, you’ve received complaints that patients are waiting too long. To investigate, you randomly sample 30 patients and record their waiting times.
Your sample shows an average waiting time of 52 minutes. But before concluding that there’s a problem, you need to ask: Is this difference of 7 minutes statistically significant, or could it simply be due to the natural variation we’d expect when taking a random sample?
This is precisely what the one-sample t-test will help us determine.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
The Formula
The t-statistic is calculated as:
\[t = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}}\]
Where:

\(\bar{X}\): sample mean (the average of your observed data)
\(\mu_0\): hypothesized/known mean (the benchmark you’re comparing against)
\(s\): sample standard deviation (measures the spread of your data)
\(n\): sample size (number of observations)


Understanding the Formula
The t-statistic essentially measures how many standard errors the sample mean is away from the hypothesized value. Let’s break this down:

The numerator (\(\bar{X} - \mu_0\)) represents the difference between what we observed and what we expected under the null hypothesis. A larger difference suggests our sample may come from a population with a different mean.
The denominator (\(s / \sqrt{n}\)) is the standard error of the mean, which tells us how much variability we’d expect in sample means due to random sampling. Dividing by this standardizes our difference, allowing us to assess whether it’s large relative to the expected sampling variation.

A t-statistic close to zero means our sample mean is close to the benchmark. A t-statistic far from zero (either positive or negative) means our sample mean differs substantially from the benchmark, relative to the variability in our data.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
Example Calculation
Let’s work through a concrete example. Suppose we collected waiting times from 30 randomly selected patients:

# Sample data: ED waiting times (minutes) from 30 patients
waiting_times <- c(47, 48, 50, 44, 49, 46, 42, 51, 45, 48,
                   44, 47, 46, 43, 48, 45, 47, 41, 49, 44,
                   50, 43, 46, 42, 47, 48, 49, 44, 46, 47)

# Calculate statistics
n <- length(waiting_times)
x_bar <- mean(waiting_times)
s <- sd(waiting_times)
mu_0 <- 45  # benchmark (regional average)

# Calculate t-statistic manually
t_stat <- (x_bar - mu_0) / (s / sqrt(n))



Sample size: 30


Sample mean: 46.2 minutes


Sample SD: 2.61 


Standard error: 0.48


t-statistic: 2.52


The t-statistic tells us how many standard errors our sample mean (approximately 46 minutes) is away from the benchmark (45 minutes). A large absolute t-value suggests the difference is unlikely to be due to chance.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
Visualizing the Null Distribution
Visualizing what we would expect to see if the null hypothesis were true (i.e., if the true population mean really were 45 minutes) helps us understand hypothesis testing. This is called the null distribution.
The graph below shows the t-distribution under the null hypothesis. The gray shaded areas in the tails represent the rejection regions; if our calculated t-statistic falls in these regions, we reject the null hypothesis at the α = 0.05 significance level.









Notice that our calculated t-statistic (the red vertical line) falls into the right rejection region. This tells us visually that our sample mean is significantly different from the benchmark (i.e., such an extreme result would be very unlikely if the true mean were actually 45 minutes).

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
Conducting in R
In practice, we use R’s built-in t.test() function rather than calculating everything manually. This function handles all the computations and provides a complete summary of results:

# Perform one-sample t-test
result <- t.test(waiting_times, mu = 45)
parameters(result)

One Sample t-test

Parameter     |  Mean | mu | Difference |         95% CI | t(29) |     p
------------------------------------------------------------------------
waiting_times | 46.20 | 45 |       1.20 | [45.23, 47.17] |  2.52 | 0.017

Alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 45



Interpreting the Output
Let’s break down what each part of the output means:

t-statistic (2.52): This measures how far our sample mean is from the hypothesized value in standard error units. Our value is quite large, indicating a substantial deviation.
df (degrees of freedom = 29): This equals n - 1 and determines the shape of the t-distribution used for calculating the p-value.
p-value (0.0174): This is the probability of observing a t-statistic as extreme as ours (or more extreme) if the null hypothesis were true. Our very small p-value indicates this would be extremely unlikely.
95% confidence interval [45.23, 47.17]: If we get samples repeatedly from the population of this sample, 95% of those samples’ mean values are expected to be within this range. Because 45 is not contained in this interval, we can reject the null hypothesis.
Sample mean (46.2): The average of our observed waiting times.



Conclusion
Since the p-value is much less than 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis. The evidence strongly suggests that the hospital’s average ED waiting time is significantly higher than the 45-minute regional standard. This finding warrants investigation into the causes of the longer wait times and potential interventions to address the issue.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
What is it?
An independent-samples t-test (also called a two-sample t-test) compares means from two different, unrelated groups to determine if they are significantly different from each other. Unlike the one-sample t-test where we compare against a fixed benchmark, here we’re asking: Are these two group means significantly different from each other, or could the observed difference be due to random variation?
This test is fundamental for comparing any two distinct groups, such as different treatment groups, different facilities, different time periods, or any other meaningful categorization. The key requirement is that the groups must be independent, meaning that the observations in one group have no relationship to the observations in the other group.

Key Requirements

Two independent groups: The observations in one group must be completely unrelated to those in the other group. (e.g., the behavior of patients at Hospital A does not influence the behavior of patients at Hospital B)
Continuous outcome variable: The variable you’re measuring (e.g., processing time, satisfaction score, length of stay) must be measured on a continuous scale.



Why “Independent”?
The term “independent” distinguishes this test from the paired-samples t-test. In an independent-samples design, each observation belongs to only one group, and there’s no natural pairing between observations across groups. If you measured the same patients before and after treatment, that would require a paired test instead.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
When to Use It
The independent-samples t-test is appropriate whenever you want to compare two separate groups. Common scenarios include:

Comparing treatments: Is a new drug more effective than the standard treatment?
Comparing facilities or departments: Does one hospital have shorter wait times than another?
Intervention studies: Did the intervention group have better outcomes than the control group?
Demographic comparisons: Do outcomes differ between urban and rural facilities?

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
Scenario: Comparing Patient Intake Systems
Imagine your health system is considering whether to invest in digital intake systems across all facilities. Currently, Hospital A uses a digital tablet-based intake system, while Hospital B uses traditional paper forms. Before making a system-wide investment, leadership wants to know: Does the digital system actually result in faster processing times?
You collect processing time data from 20 randomly selected patients at each hospital. The question is whether any difference you observe represents a significant difference in system efficiency, or whether it could simply be due to natural variation in processing times.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
The Formula
The t-statistic for an independent-samples t-test is calculated as:
\[t = \frac{\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2}{s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}}\]
Where the pooled standard deviation is:
\[s_p = \sqrt{\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2 + (n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}}\]

Understanding the Formula

Numerator (\(\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2\)): The difference between the two sample means, which is the effect we are trying to evaluate.
Denominator: The standard error of the difference between means. This combines the information about variability from both groups to estimate how much variation we would expect in the difference between sample means due to random sampling.
Pooled standard deviation (\(s_p\)): This is a weighted average of the two groups’ standard deviations. We “pool” them because we assume both groups have the same population variance (homogeneity of variance assumption). The pooling gives more weight to the larger sample.

The resulting t-statistic tells us how many standard errors the observed difference is from zero (i.e., no difference; the same mean in both groups). A large absolute t-value suggests the groups significantly differ.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
What is it?
A paired-samples t-test (also called a dependent t-test or matched-pairs t-test) compares two related measurements on the same subjects or matched pairs. Unlike the independent-samples t-test where we compare different groups of people, here we’re asking: Is there a significant change within the same individuals between two time points, conditions, or measures?
This test is particularly powerful because by measuring the same subjects twice, we can control for individual differences. Each person serves as their own control, which reduces variability and increases our ability to detect true effects.

Key Characteristic
The data comes in pairs, which means each subject has exactly two measurements that are linked. For example:

The same patient measured before and after treatment
The same clinic’s performance in January vs. June
Twins where one receives treatment and the other serves as control



Why Use Paired Data?
The paired design is statistically more powerful than an independent design because it eliminates the variability across respondents. For example, if we compare pain scores between a treatment group and control group (independent design), differences in pain tolerance between individuals add noise to our data. But if we measure each person’s pain before and after treatment (paired design), individual differences cancel out, and we are only looking at how much each person’s pain perceptions changed.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
When to Use It
The paired-samples t-test is appropriate whenever your measurements are somehow related:

Before-and-after studies (same respondent):

Pre-treatment vs. post-treatment outcomes
Before vs. after policy implementation
Baseline vs. follow-up measurements

Matched pairs design:

Twin studies (comparing outcomes between twins)
Matched control studies (subjects paired on key characteristics)

Within-subject comparisons:

Two treatments tested on the same patient (crossover design)
Morning vs. evening measurements on the same individuals
Left eye vs. right eye comparisons

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
Scenario: Pain Management Protocol
A hospital implemented a new pain management protocol and wants to evaluate its effectiveness. Rather than comparing different groups of patients (which would introduce confounding variables like age, health status, or pain tolerance), the hospital measures pain scores (0-10 scale) for 30 patients before and after receiving the protocol.
The key question is: Did the protocol significantly reduce pain? By using the same patients as their own controls, we can isolate the effect of the protocol from individual differences in pain perception and tolerance.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:
The Formula
The paired t-test analyzes the differences between paired observations:
\[t = \frac{\bar{D}}{s_D / \sqrt{n}}\]
Where:

\(\bar{D}\): mean of the differences (average change across all subjects)
\(s_D\): standard deviation of the differences (variability in how much individuals changed)
\(n\): number of pairs (number of subjects)


Understanding the Formula
Notice that this formula is essentially identical to the one-sample t-test formula! This is because the paired t-test is really just a one-sample t-test performed on the differences. We’re testing whether the mean difference is significantly different from zero.
Instead of working with two sets of measurements (e.g., average before - average after), we first calculate the difference for each pair (e.g., Before - After for each patient). Then we examine whether the average of these differences significantly different from zero.

If the mean difference is close to zero → no significant difference
If the mean difference is far from zero (relative to variability) → significant difference

This approach is powerful because it accounts for individual baseline differences. A patient who starts with severe pain and a patient who starts with mild pain are compared only to themselves.

title: Mean Comparison 1: t-Tests
text:

# Pain scores before and after intervention
before <- c(7, 8, 6, 7, 7, 8, 6, 7, 8, 7,

           7, 5, 8, 6, 6, 8, 6, 6, 7, 7,
           6, 7, 7, 5, 7, 7, 7, 7, 6, 7)

Conducting in R
We can conduct a paired-sample t-test using t.test() function with the paired = TRUE argument:

# Perform paired samples t-test
result_paired <- t.test(before, after, paired = TRUE)
parameters(result_paired)

Paired t-test

Parameter | Group | Difference | t(29) |     p |       95% CI
-------------------------------------------------------------
before    | after |       0.40 |  2.84 | 0.008 | [0.11, 0.69]

Alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0



Interpretation

Mean difference: 0.4 points
t-statistic: 2.845
p-value: 0.01
Conclusion: Since p-value < 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis. The pain management protocol significantly reduced pain scores.

Widely used in academia and industry, especially in healthcare analytics

Discuss the advantages of using R and R-Studio for healthcare data analysis. Mention its open-source nature and strong community support.

R and R-Studio
The popularity of data science software

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this session, you should be able to:

Distinguish between populations, samples, and sub-populations
Identify appropriate distributions for different healthcare outcomes
Explain conditional vs. marginal means
Understand overdispersion and between-individual heterogeneity
Critically interpret p-values and hypothesis tests
Recognize common pitfalls in statistical inference


This chapter provides essential statistical foundations for analyzing healthcare data. Emphasize that healthcare outcomes rarely follow normal distributions, which motivates much of the material.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Populations and Samples
Population: The complete group we want to learn about

Well-defined (e.g., all Hiroshima atomic bomb survivors who survived 1+ years)
Can be hypothetical (e.g., all breast cancer patients who have/will undergo mastectomy)

Sample: A subset of the population used for inference

Random samples enable quantification of uncertainty
Many healthcare studies use convenience samples or complete censuses

Sub-population: A population subset satisfying specific criteria

Defined by fixed characteristics (e.g., men under 20 in Hiroshima cohort)
Regression models estimate means for sub-populations defined by covariates


Emphasize that representativeness is always a concern, regardless of how samples are obtained. Discuss how this relates to external validity.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Random Variables in Healthcare
Healthcare outcomes are random variables that vary across individuals:

Binary: Re-admission after surgery (Yes/No)
Categorical: Treatment type (surgery/radiation/hormonal)
Count: Number of outpatient visits, prescriptions filled
Continuous: Medical expenditures, length of stay

Notation: - Capital letters (X, Y) for generic/theoretical variables - Lowercase letters (x, y) for specific observed values

Give concrete examples from students’ experience. Ask: What healthcare outcomes have they encountered? What types of variables are these?

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Dependent vs. Independent Variables
Research Question Determines the Relationship

Dependent variable (Y): Outcome or response
Independent variable (X): Predictor or covariate

Example: Exercise and insomnia

Exercise may reduce insomnia → Exercise is X, insomnia is Y
Insomnia may reduce exercise ability → Insomnia is X, exercise is Y
Both may be true (feedback loop) → Modeling challenge!

Key principle: Variables that co-evolve should often both be considered outcomes

Discuss the importance of conceptual models (like Andersen-Newman) in sorting out variable relationships. Medical expenditures and hospitalizations example from the text.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Statistical Distributions
A distribution describes the probability that a variable takes any value in its range
For categorical variables: Finite set of probabilities (sum to 1)
For continuous variables: Probability density function (PDF)

Area under PDF over an interval = probability of value in that interval
Cumulative distribution function (CDF) = probability ≤ specified value

Key summaries: - Mean (expected value): Most typical value, influenced by extremes - Median (50th percentile): Center of distribution, robust to outliers

Healthcare data is often right-skewed, so median may be more representative than mean. Show the MEPS expenditure histogram from Figure 2.1.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
MEPS Total Expenditure Example


Mean: $18,145
Median: $9,664
Extreme right skew with long tail
Mean > Median indicates right skewness


This is typical of healthcare expenditure data. A few high-cost users drive up the mean substantially above the median.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Parameters and Models
Parameters: Greek letters (μ, σ, α, β) that specify a distribution

Normal distribution: mean μ, variance σ²
Parametric methods: specify family, estimate parameters

Models: Assumptions and mathematical specifications for analysis

Rarely unique - multiple models may address same question
Model choice affects both estimates and their standard errors
What constitutes a “good model” is a recurring theme


Emphasize that model assumptions matter greatly. Healthcare outcomes often violate normality assumption, motivating specialized distributions.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Estimation and Inference
Estimation: Using sample data to learn about population

Sample mean estimates population mean
Sample median estimates population median

Statistical Inference: Using estimates to answer research questions

Combines estimates with their uncertainty (standard errors)
Hypothesis tests are one tool for inference

Standard Error (SE): Quantifies variation over repeated samples

Higher SE → greater expected variation
Decreases with larger sample size
Depends on the model used


Different models can yield similar point estimates but very different standard errors, affecting inference. Preview the two-part model discussion from Chapter 6.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Conditional vs. Marginal Means
MEPS 2017 Expenditures by Health Status



Health Status
% of Sample
Expenditures




Excellent
34%
$1,957


Very good
29%
$3,729


Good
25%
$6,183


Fair
10%
$11,387


Poor
3%
$22,619




This table illustrates both conditional and marginal means. Each expenditure is conditional on health status.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Conditional vs. Marginal Means (cont.)
Conditional mean: \(E(Y | X = x)\) - mean for specific sub-population

\(E(Y | \text{Excellent}) = \$1,957\)
\(E(Y | \text{Poor}) = \$22,619\)

Marginal mean: \(E(Y)\) - weighted average across all sub-populations
\[E(Y) = 1957(0.34) + 3729(0.29) + 6183(0.25) + 11387(0.10) + 22619(0.03)\] \[= \$5,110\]
Lower than highest categories because healthier (lower-cost) people are more common!

This is a crucial concept for regression. Marginal mean averages over the distribution of X. Emphasize that weights matter.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Bernoulli and Binomial Distributions
Bernoulli: Binary outcome (0 or 1)

Parameter: \(p = P(Y = 1)\)
Mean: \(E(Y) = p\)
Variance: \(Var(Y) = p(1-p)\)
Variance depends on mean!

Binomial: Sum of n independent Bernoulli variables

Parameters: n (number of trials), p (success probability)
Mean: \(np\)
Variance: \(np(1-p)\)

Example: Hospital re-admissions after surgery

Binary prediction is a classification problem. Statistical learning has different algorithms for this (Chapter 10). Emphasize that binomial requires independence - clustering violates this.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Binomial Distribution

Shape depends on both n and p. As n increases, distribution becomes more bell-shaped.

Show how the distribution changes with parameters. When p=0.5 and n is large, it approaches normal distribution (Central Limit Theorem preview).

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Multinomial Distribution
Generalization of binomial for multiple categories (K > 2)
Examples:

Treatment choice: surgery/radiation/hormonal (3 unordered categories)
Health status: excellent/very good/good/fair/poor (5 ordered categories)

Parameters: K-1 independent probabilities (must sum to 1)
Analysis Goal: Identify factors predicting probability of each category

How does diabetes affect \(P(Y = k)\) for each health status category k?


Ordered vs. unordered categories require different modeling approaches. Can treat ordered as continuous or use ordinal regression methods.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Poisson Distribution for Counts
Basic distribution for count data (0, 1, 2, 3, …)
Assumptions: - Events occur at constant rate - Memoryless (past doesn’t affect future probability)
Parameter: λ (mean rate)
Key property: Mean = Variance = λ
Highly restrictive for healthcare data!

Show Figure 2.3. The equal mean-variance assumption is almost always violated in practice. Healthcare counts typically show overdispersion.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Poisson Distribution


As λ increases, distribution becomes more symmetric and bell-shaped.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Overdispersion in Healthcare Data

Observed MEPS outpatient visits vs. Simulated Poisson

Observed: Mean = 1.5, Variance = 24 (16× mean!)
More zeros and longer right tail than Poisson predicts


This is typical of healthcare utilization data. Poisson assumption is too restrictive. Need alternative models.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Negative Binomial Distribution
Accommodates overdispersion: Variance > Mean
Mechanism: Between-individual heterogeneity

Each person has their own latent “frailty” or “susceptibility”
Some rarely seek care (low frailty), others frequently (high frailty)
Individual’s conditional mean: \(\mu r_i\) (where \(r_i\) is personal frailty)

Result: If frailties follow gamma distribution with mean 1, variance α - Marginal distribution of Y is negative binomial - Mean: μ - Variance: \(\mu(1 + \alpha\mu)\) > \(\mu\)

This latent heterogeneity concept recurs in random effects and frailty models. Emphasize that it’s a specific mechanism for overdispersion.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Normal Distribution
Symmetric, bell-shaped distribution
Parameters: mean μ, standard deviation σ
Key properties: - 67% of observations within 1 SD of mean - 95% within 2 SDs - Values >2 SDs away are “atypical”
Standardization: \(Z = (Y - \mu)/\sigma\) has mean 0, SD 1

Show Figure 2.5. Most healthcare outcomes are NOT normal, but the normal is crucial because of the Central Limit Theorem - sample means are approximately normal.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Normal Distribution


Different σ values show different spreads. The distribution is completely determined by μ and σ.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Central Limit Theorem
Key insight: Even if data are non-normal, sample means are approximately normal

Distribution of sample mean \(\bar{Y}\) approaches normal as n increases
True regardless of the distribution of Y itself
Enables hypothesis testing based on normal approximation

Crucial distinction: - Population data distribution: Often non-normal in healthcare - Sample estimate distribution: Approximately normal

This is why we can use normal-based inference even with skewed healthcare data. But this applies to the sampling distribution of estimates, not the data itself.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Gamma Distribution
Flexible distribution for non-negative, continuous, right-skewed outcomes
Parameters: α (shape), β (rate)

Mean: α/β
Variance: α/β²

Can accommodate various shapes from highly skewed to more symmetric
Commonly used for medical expenditures

Show Figure 2.6. The gamma is quite flexible and can match many right-skewed distributions. The variance can be greater or less than the mean.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Gamma Distribution


As α increases (for fixed β), the distribution becomes more symmetric and bell-shaped.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Lognormal Distribution
Y has lognormal distribution if log(Y) has normal distribution
If \(\log(Y) \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\), then:
\[E(Y) = \exp\left(\mu + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\right) \neq \exp(\mu)\]
Critical point: Order of operations matters!

\(E[\log(Y)] \neq \log[E(Y)]\)
Retransformation is not straightforward

Usage: Any log-transformed regression implicitly assumes lognormal outcomes

This retransformation issue is a major challenge in cost regression (Chapter 6). Show Table 2.2 from MEPS data.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Retransformation Problem
MEPS 2017 Example



Expense Type

Cannot simply exponentiate the mean of logged values!
Correction factor needed: \(\exp(\sigma^2/2)\)

This is a common mistake. Emphasize that quantiles (like median) do transform directly, which motivates quantile regression.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Lognormal Distribution

Right-skewed with heavy right tail, suitable for expenditure data

Different σ values control the degree of skewness. Larger σ → heavier tail.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Hypothesis Testing Framework
Purpose: Reach decision about hypothesis while quantifying error risk
Structure: - Null hypothesis \(H_0\): typically what we want to disprove - Alternative \(H_A\): what we believe - Test statistic from sample data - P-value: probability of observed data (or more extreme) if \(H_0\) is true
Decision: - Reject \(H_0\) if p-value is small - Cannot “accept” \(H_0\), only “fail to reject”

Emphasize the one-way nature. Absence of evidence ≠ evidence of absence. This asymmetry is fundamental to the framework.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
What P-values Actually Mean
P-value: Probability of observing data as or more extreme than what we saw, assuming \(H_0\) is true
Common misconception: P-value = probability that \(H_0\) is true ❌
Correct interpretation: P-value quantifies how inconsistent the data are with \(H_0\)

Low p-value → data unlikely under \(H_0\) → reject \(H_0\)
High p-value → data not inconsistent with \(H_0\) → cannot conclude anything


This is the most common misinterpretation. P-value is a statement about the data, not about the hypothesis. Many published papers get this wrong.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Problems with P-value Thresholds
Traditional “rule”: p < 0.05 = “statistically significant”
Problems:

Large samples: Trivial effects can have tiny p-values

Effect size ≈ 0 but p < 0.001

Small samples: Important effects may have large p-values

Low statistical power

Multiple comparisons: Error rate inflates

5 tests: P(at least 1 false positive) = 0.23
10 tests: P(at least 1 false positive) = 0.40

Invites p-hacking: Manipulation to achieve p < 0.05


ASA statement (2016) and many journals now discourage bright-line thresholds. Focus on effect sizes and confidence intervals instead.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
section: P-hacking and Researcher Degrees of Freedom
text:
P-hacking and Researcher Degrees of Freedom
P-hacking: Trying multiple analyses until finding p < 0.05
Methods: - Selective reporting of results - Choosing convenient exclusion criteria - Dichotomizing continuous variables at chosen cut-points - Dropping certain missing data patterns - Choosing specific statistical tests
Solution: Pre-specify analysis plan, report all analyses conducted
Best practice: Focus on effect sizes and practical significance

With large healthcare databases, this is especially tempting and problematic. Reproducibility crisis in science partly stems from this.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Multiple Comparisons Problem
Example: Testing 10 covariates individually for association with expenditures

Each test at α = 0.05
P(at least 1 false positive) = \(1 - (0.95)^{10} = 0.40\)

Solutions:

Bonferroni correction: Test each at α/k level
False discovery rate: Control proportion of false positives
Pre-specification: Develop strong conceptual model first


In genomic studies with thousands of tests, this is critical. But even with 5-10 tests, the problem is real. Conceptual models help limit number of tests.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Best Practices for Inference
Do: - Report effect sizes with confidence intervals - Consider practical significance alongside statistical significance - Acknowledge uncertainty in p-values themselves - Pre-specify hypotheses when possible - Report all analyses conducted - Consider multiple comparison adjustments
Don’t: - Treat p = 0.049 differently from p = 0.051 - Conclude \(H_0\) is true from large p-value - Interpret p-value as P(\(H_0\) is true) - Hide analyses that didn’t achieve p < 0.05

Growing recognition in scientific community of these limitations. Many journals now require pre-registration of analysis plans. Emphasize reproducibility.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Key Takeaways

Healthcare outcomes require specialized distributions (not just normal)
Understand overdispersion and between-individual heterogeneity
Conditional vs. marginal estimation is fundamental to regression
Transformation requires careful retransformation
P-values are widely misunderstood - focus on effect sizes
Standard errors matter as much as point estimates
Model assumptions affect both estimates and inference


These concepts form the foundation for regression methods in subsequent chapters. Emphasize that appropriate distribution choice is driven by outcome type.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Looking Ahead
Chapter 3: Data visualization

Preview that many of the distributions covered today will have corresponding regression methods. The regression model specifies how the parameters of these distributions depend on covariates.

Academic Integrity and ChatGPT/AI Generated Content
As a student at UD, you are expected to adhere to the Standards of Conduct outlined in the Academic Honor Code. One of the goals for your educational development is to develop your critical thinking and writing skills, which can be weakened by regularly utilizing AI for writing. Thus, for this course, all submitted writing should be your own, original work. If you quote or copy content from ChatGPT or other AI sources, it must be appropriately cited in your submissions. As your instructor, I am required to investigate all suspected violations of academic dishonesty and follow the honor code violation procedures, which can result in an NC for the course.

title: Week 3: Basic Statistical Concepts
text:
By the end of this module, you will be able to:

Identify the four scales of measurement and select appropriate statistics for each
Calculate and interpret measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode) and dispersion (range, variance, standard deviation)
Recognize how data distribution shapes affect the choice of central tendency measures
Understand the logic of null hypothesis significance testing
Interpret p-values correctly and avoid common misconceptions
Apply these concepts to healthcare management decision-making

title: Week 3: Basic Statistical Concepts
text:
2.1 Why Measurement Scales Matter
In healthcare management, we collect many types of data: patient demographics, satisfaction scores, diagnosis codes, length of stay, and costs. How we measure something determines which statistical analyses are appropriate and meaningful.






ImportantKey Principle



Scales of measurement are NOT about “what” is measured, but about “how” something is measured. The same concept (like patient age) can be measured using different scales.

title: Week 3: Basic Statistical Concepts
text:
2.2 The Four Scales

scales_data <- tibble(
  Scale = factor(c("Nominal", "Ordinal", "Interval", "Ratio"),
                 levels = c("Nominal", "Ordinal", "Interval", "Ratio")),
  Information = c(1, 2, 3, 4),
  Label = c("Categories\nonly", "Categories +\nOrder", "Categories +\nOrder +\nEqual intervals",
            "Categories +\nOrder +\nEqual intervals +\nTrue zero")
)

ggplot(scales_data, aes(x = Scale, y = Information, fill = Scale)) +

geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Label), vjust = -0.3, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#E8E8E8", "#B8D4E8", "#6BAED6", "#2171B5")) +
  labs(title = "Measurement Scales: From Less to More Information",
       y = "Amount of Information") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.text.y = element_blank()) +
  ylim(0, 5.5)







Figure 1: Hierarchy of Measurement Scales

title: Week 3: Basic Statistical Concepts
text:
2.3 Nominal Scale
Definition: Numbers or labels indicate different categories or groups with no inherent order.

2.3.1 Healthcare Examples

Diagnosis codes: ICD-10 codes (e.g., I50.9 for Heart Failure, J18.9 for Pneumonia)
Insurance type: Private, Medicare, Medicaid, Uninsured
Hospital department: Emergency, Surgery, Internal Medicine
Blood type: A, B, AB, O


patient_satisfaction %>%
  count(insurance_type) %>%
  mutate(Percentage = round(n/sum(n)*100, 1)) %>%
  rename(`Insurance Type` = insurance_type, Count = n) %>%
  kable() %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))

2.3.2 Appropriate Statistics for Nominal Data

Central tendency: Mode (most frequent category)
Dispersion: Frequency distribution, percentages







WarningCommon Mistake



You CANNOT calculate a meaningful mean or median for nominal data. Even if categories are coded as numbers (1, 2, 3, 4), the average is meaningless!
Example: If Private=1, Medicare=2, Medicaid=3, Uninsured=4, an “average” of 2.3 has no interpretation.

title: Week 3: Basic Statistical Concepts
text:
2.4 Ordinal Scale
Definition: Numbers indicate relative order or rank, but intervals between values are not necessarily equal.

2.4.1 Healthcare Examples

Pain scale categories: None, Mild, Moderate, Severe
Age groups: 18-44, 45-64, 65-74, 75+
NYHA Heart Failure Class: I, II, III, IV
Triage categories: Immediate, Emergent, Urgent, Less Urgent, Non-Urgent
Satisfaction categories: Very Dissatisfied, Dissatisfied, Neutral, Satisfied, Very Satisfied


readmission_data %>%
  mutate(age_group = factor(age_group, levels = c("18-44", "45-64", "65-74", "75+"))) %>%
  count(age_group) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group, y = n, fill = age_group)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), vjust = -0.5) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues") +
  labs(title = "Patient Age Group Distribution",
       x = "Age Group", y = "Number of Patients") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")







Figure 2: Distribution of Age Groups in Readmission Data







2.4.2 Appropriate Statistics for Ordinal Data

Central tendency: Mode (for categories), Median (for ranks)
Dispersion: Frequency distribution, Range

title: Week 3: Basic Statistical Concepts
text:
2.5 Interval Scale
Definition: Equal intervals between scale points, but no true zero point. Differences are meaningful, but ratios are not.

2.5.1 Healthcare Examples

Satisfaction scores (1-7 scale with equal intervals assumed)
Temperature (Fahrenheit or Celsius)
Year of diagnosis
Likert-type scales used in patient surveys


ggplot(patient_satisfaction, aes(x = factor(satisfaction_score))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#2171B5") +
  geom_text(stat = "count", aes(label = after_stat(count)), vjust = -0.5) +
  labs(title = "Patient Satisfaction Score Distribution",
       subtitle = "1 = Very Dissatisfied, 7 = Very Satisfied",
       x = "Satisfaction Score", y = "Number of Patients") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 3: Distribution of Patient Satisfaction Scores (1-7 Scale)







2.5.2 Appropriate Statistics for Interval Data

Central tendency: Mode, Median, Mean
Dispersion: Frequency distribution, Range, Variance/Standard Deviation







NoteQuasi-Interval Scales



Many healthcare surveys use Likert-type scales (e.g., 5-point or 7-point scales) that are technically ordinal but often treated as interval. This is acceptable when:

Scale has 5+ points
Labels suggest equal spacing
Statistical tradition supports it (e.g., HCAHPS surveys)

title: Week 3: Basic Statistical Concepts
text:
2.6 Ratio Scale
Definition: Has all properties of interval scale plus a true zero point. Ratios between values are meaningful.

2.6.1 Healthcare Examples

Length of stay (days)
Wait time (minutes)
Total charges ($)
Number of comorbidities
Readmission rate (%)
Age (years)
Blood pressure (mmHg)


ggplot(patient_satisfaction, aes(x = length_of_stay)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#2171B5", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Length of Stay Distribution",
       subtitle = "Note: Right-skewed distribution typical of LOS data",
       x = "Length of Stay (Days)", y = "Number of Patients") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 4: Distribution of Length of Stay (Days)







2.6.2 Appropriate Statistics for Ratio Data

Central tendency: Mode, Median, Mean
Dispersion: Frequency distribution, Range, Variance/Standard Deviation

Key difference from interval: You CAN make meaningful ratio statements.

“Hospital A’s average LOS (6 days) is twice that of Hospital B (3 days).”
